Preamble
“… The United Nations of the twenty-first century must continue to be
guided by its founding principles. It must remain an Organization
dedicated to the interests of its Member States and of their peoples. Our
objectives will not change: peace, prosperity, social justice and a
sustainable future. But the means we use to achieve those ends must be
adapted to the challenges of the new era.”

Foreword
The United Nations Development Assistance Framework (UNDAF) is an essential component of the
United Nations programme for reform introduced by the UN Secretary-General in July 1997. As a
strategic planning framework for UN development cooperation and assistance at the country level, the
UNDAF provides a strong basis for increased collaboration and impact of development assistance, as well
as a framework under which the UN organizations support long-term national development goals.
The UNDAF for the Lao PDR, 2002-2006, is a UN document prepared in close consultation between the
UN Country Team and the Government of the Lao PDR, and it is based on the findings and
recommendations of the UN Common Country Assessment (CCA) 2000.
The four UNDAF focus areas for the Lao PDR – development and poverty eradication policies and
strategies; response to basic human needs; sustainable use of natural resources and preservation of cultural
heritage; and human rights, gender equality and good governance – reflect a convergence of national
needs and priorities, and the areas to which UN development assistance, and the assistance of the
International Financial Institutions that are members of the UNCT in the Lao PDR, can be effectively
applied.
The goals and objectives contained in this document aim to assist the Government of the Lao PDR realize
its long-term development goals, in support of its socio-economic development strategy and vision for the
years 2000-2002, including the determination of the Lao PDR to poverty reduction and to leave the status
of Least Developed Country by the year 2020. The UNDAF for the Lao PDR builds upon the
considerable social and economic achievements of the country and represent the values espoused by the
United Nations, by the Bretton Woods Institutions and by the Asian Development Bank, as embodied in
UN conventions, international covenants and declarations, and in the Millennium Development Goals.
By developing and implementing the UNDAF, it is hoped to have broadened the understanding of the
work of the UN System, the Bretton Woods Institutions and the Asian Development Bank in the Lao
PDR, and clarified its relationships and partnerships with the Government and the donor community in
order to utilize more effectively ODA resources.
Many Government ministries, senior officials, mass organizations have provided valuable contributions
and active participation in the development of this document and in the UNDAF process itself. It is
hoped that the UNDAF will provide the basis for further deepening cooperation and partnership in the
coming yeas to meet the development challenges and opportunities of the Lao PDR.
Somsavat Lengsavad
Deputy Prime Minister,
Minister of Foreign Affairs
Kari Nordheim-Larsen
United Nations
Resident Coordinator
2 July 20024
Mission Statement
We, the United Nations Country Team in the Lao PDR, are determined to support the national
development goal of eradicating mass poverty through sustainable and equitable socio-economic
development with a human perspective. Our mission is to help the Government and people of the Lao
PDR in their fight against poverty by addressing the multi-facetted causes of poverty from the policymaking and community levels, ensuring rights-based approach to development, supporting the sustainable
use of natural resources and preservation of cultural heritage, and promoting human rights, gender
equality and good governance.
Guided by the national development needs and priorities, the global Millennium Development Goals, and
principles embodied in the UN Charter and other fundamental UN instruments, we will strive to provide
the best advice and strengthen national institutional and human resource capacities and ownership. We
will target our assistance at the most vulnerable and poor, in particular women, children and youth, and
rural population.
While supporting the Lao PDR’s development goals, we are committed to using this UN Development
Assistance Framework process as an opportunity for closer collaboration among the Government, UN
System, Bretton Woods Institutions, ADB, and a broader development community: bilateral donors,
international NGOs, mass organization, civil society and the private sector.
Respecting the specific identities and mandates of our organizations, we aim to improve our coordination,
effectiveness and efficiency, to reinforce the impact of our assistance, and to provide the best possible
service to the Government and people of the Lao PDR.

UNITED NATIONS DEVELOPMENT ASSISTANCE FRAMEWORK
FOR THE LAO PDR 2002-2006
I. Executive Summary
The United Nations Development Assistance Framework (UNDAF) is a strategic planning and
collaborative programming framework mandated in the UN Secretary-General’s Programme for Reform,
July 1997. It outlines the main goals, objectives and cooperation strategies for the UN assistance during
the next 5 years. The UNDAF draws on the key development issues and challenges identified in the
Common Country Assessment (CCA). At the same time, each of the UNDAF goals directly responds to
the national development needs and priorities, as well as supports the realization of commitments deriving
from the world conferences, global summits, and international treaties, including the Millennium
Declaration.
The overarching goal of the UN Country Team in the Lao PDR from 2002-2006 is to provide support to
the national development needs and priorities, and promote the implementation of the declarations
and programmes of action of the world conferences and international conventions, including the
human rights instruments, to which the Lao PDR is a State party. In doing so, the UN will pursue
the following goals:
Goal 1: Development and Poverty Eradication
Policies and Strategies
• Face up to regionalization, internationalization
and globalization
• Develop a comprehensive national policy
environment
• Develop an enabling macroeconomic
environment, and strengthen and deepen the
reform process
• Strengthen aid coordination and reduce aid
dependency
• Ensure adequate resource allocation and
sustainable financing for social and human
development
• Address the imbalance in capital and current
expenditure
• Ensure fully integrated and coordinated poverty
reduction strategies and programmes
Goal 2: Response to Basic Human Needs
• Develop sustainable livelihoods and ensuring
household food security
• Meet basic household needs
• Ensure equal access to basic education of good
quality with a special focus on girls education
• Promote sound population development
(reproductive health)
• Improve health status of the population
• Prevent an HIV/AIDS epidemic
• Eliminate opium production, drug abuse and
drug trafficking
• Remove UXO contamination
Goal 3: Sustainable Use of Natural Resources
and Preservation of Cultural Heritage
• Ensure the sustainable use of natural resources
and preservation of cultural heritage
Goal 4: Human Rights, Gender Equality and
Good Governance
• Promote human rights for all
• Improve child rights and care and reduce child
and youth vulnerability
• Ensure growth with equity (reduce disparities
related to gender, ethnicity, location and
returnee status)
• Deepen participation and broaden partnerships
• Build institutional and administrative capacityUnited Nations Development Assistance Framework for the Lao PDR 2002-2006
11
• Strengthen human resource capacity
• Improve the collection, analysis and
dissemination of data/ information/ knowledge
The UN Country Team will also be guided by a number of UNDAF-based principles:
• Promote national ownership of programmes and projects through sustainable capacity building and
enabling people’s participation.
• Apply human rights-based approach to development that
- focuses on people as holders of rights, as well as duties and responsibilities;
- adopts the fundamental principles of non-discrimination;
- prioritizes needs of the most disadvantaged and vulnerable;
- reiterates that development is a human right; and
- targets the goal of poverty eradication by addressing structural inequalities that cause
poverty.
• Mainstream gender issues and promote gender equality.
• Incorporate sub-regional and regional issues into development programmes to enable
the Lao PDR’s regional and global integration.
• Implement actions of the UN Secretary-General’s Programme for Reform to
enhance inter-agency coordination/ collaboration in both operational and
programme matters.
• Pursue meaningful partnerships among all development stakeholders: the
Government, UN System, BWIs, ADB, bi- and multilateral donors, civil
society, and the private sector.
The UN collaboration in the Lao PDR will take a form of a mix of agency-specific, complementary,
parallel, and joint programmes and projects. The UN Country Team will review opportunities for
developing parallel and joint programmes where they add value, while the prevailing form of UN agency
collaboration will be a set of agency-specific or complementary programmes. Strategic approaches to
collaboration will vary for each development intervention. In course of the UNDAF preparation, the UN
Country Team identified tentative cooperation strategies in most areas, which will be further detailed and
strengthened during the implementation, follow-up and review stages.
Several regular mechanisms for inter-agency coordination and collaboration are employed to ensure more
integrated, complementary action on both programme and administrative matters. These include monthly
UN Country Team (UNCT) and Security Management Team (SMT) meetings, the UN theme/working
groups, Inter-Agency Admin. Officers meetings, and the Office of the Resident Coordinator.
The UNDAF must be a living document, able to adapt itself to the country’s development challenges in a
changing environment. It will be implemented, monitored, reviewed and revised through the individual
agency country programmes and projects, as well as complementary mechanisms and processes. The
UNDAF will be used as a platform for advocacy and policy dialogue. Both the CCA and UNDAF have a
potential to generate value-added, enabling the UN to better support aid coordination. Finally, the
UNDAF should ultimately help to harmonize rules and procedures by simplifying the requirements of
individual organizations for programming and operational processes.
Effective follow-up on the UNDAF requires the establishment of adequate mechanisms for sustained
dialogue, planning and review among the Government, UN System and key development partners. In
addition to mechanisms already in place, the UNDAF Monitoring Group will be established and charged
with the role of following-up on all matters related to the implementation and monitoring of the UNDAF.
Please see the tentative TOR in chapter V A.6.United Nations Development Assistance Framework for the Lao PDR 2002-2006
12
Monitoring/ evaluation of the UNDAF by the participating UN organizations and the Government will
focus on: the extent to which the UNDAF has fulfilled its basic purpose; extent of progress towards
meeting the goals and objectives; enhanced partnerships within the UN System and with the Government
and other development partners; and progress in harmonization and streamlining of programming and
operational procedures. The UNDAF monitoring will be carried out in conjunction with the preparation
and review of the Workplans and Annual Reports of the Resident Coordinator System, and the mid-term
reviews of country programmes of cooperation. Final evaluation will take place at the end of the
UNDAF cycle.United Nations Development Assistance Framework for the Lao PDR 2002-2006
13
II. Rationale
A. UNDAF Purpose and Process
A strategic planning and collaborative programming framework, the UN Development Assistance
Framework (UNDAF) was first mandated in the UN Secretary-General’s report “Renewing the United
Nations: A Programme for Reform” of 14 July 1997, and endorsed by the UN General Assembly in
resolution 53/192. The UNDAF is designed to bring greater coherence, collaboration and effectiveness to
United Nations development efforts in the field for improving the well-being of people served by the
organization. It helps to identify priorities for the United Nations action in close collaboration with the
Government and development partners. In short, the UNDAF identifies common challenges, common
responses, common resource frameworks, and potential partnerships.
In such collaboration, the UNDAF – both as a process and a product – is based on the Common Country
Assessment (CCA) and linked with a number of other key instruments of development cooperation,
employed by the UN System and its partners, including the Country Strategy Note, Comprehensive
Development Framework of the World Bank, Poverty Reduction Strategy Paper and Round Table
Meeting processes, as well as reporting on the Millennium Development Goals.
The CCA is a country-based process for reviewing and analyzing the national development situation using
a strategic approach. The CCA identifies key issues as a basis for advocacy, policy dialogue, and
preparation of a common United Nations response. The underlying rationale of the CCA is to achieve a
deeper knowledge and understanding of the country’s development challenges among the UN System,
Government, donors and civil society. The CCA process also serves to facilitate efforts for more
coherent, coordinated and integrated UN support at the country level, whilst ensuring flexibility in
adjusting to the changing circumstances. The CCA document contains an in-depth development analysis,
information on the status of follow-up to UN-sponsored world conferences, and a common indicator
framework, including national quantitative and qualitative sex-disaggregated data.
The UN Country Team in the Lao PDR completed its first CCA in October 2001. During the CCA
exercise, the three overarching themes of governance, poverty and human rights were identified and
addressed from three specific view points: socio-economic management, community participation, and
household security. These three major areas formed the basis for the UNDAF first draft reviewed by the
Government and UN Country Team at a CCA/UNDAF workshop in August 2001. In light of the
feedback received, and the latest guidance from UNDG concerning the monitoring of national progress
towards the Millennium Development Goals, the UNDAF initial structure was modified to ensure closer
correlation with both the national and global development goals.
Following extensive consultations, agreement was reached on the four major goals – (1) development and
poverty eradication policies and strategies; (2) response to basic human needs; (3) sustainable use of
natural resources and preservation of cultural heritage; and (4) human rights, gender equality and
good governance – as a basis for the UNDAF Lao PDR 2002-2006. The UNDAF draws heavily on the
findings and recommendations of the CCA and, essentially, on the key development issues and
challenges. At the same time, the document is fully in line with the national development priorities and
goals, and the Millennium Development Goals. Working from this foundation, the UN agencies jointly
identified the main goals, objectives and cooperation strategies for the UN assistance during the next 5-
year harmonized programme cycle.United Nations Development Assistance Framework for the Lao PDR 2002-2006
14
More specifically, each of the UNDAF goals:
• Responds to key issues/challenges identified in the CCA;
• Supports the national development priorities and goals (outlined in the National Socio-Economic
Development Plans and Strategies to 2005, 2010 and 2020, 7th Round Table Meeting strategies,
Interim Poverty Reduction Strategy Paper, and other key policy and strategy documents of the
Government); and
• Supports the attainment of the relevant Millennium Declaration Goals (attached in Annex E). Indeed,
the UNDAF Lao PDR reflects the larger Millennium Declaration Goals, which not only fully
incorporate all of the Millennium Development Goals, but extend further to include other important
goals (such as peace, security and disarmament – in particular eliminating UXO and drugs,
development and poverty eradication, protecting our common environment, human rights, democracy
and good governance, and protecting the vulnerable).
Guided by these goals, the rationale behind the UNDAF process remains to increase the collaboration
among the UN System, Government of the Lao PDR, and a wider donor community. The UN
collaboration, employing a holistic and multi-sectoral approach to development, will not only enhance the
impact of the UN development operations in a cost effective manner, but, most importantly, maximize
benefits to the Lao PDR.
B. Millennium Development Goals
Since 1990, the United Nations have sponsored a series of world summits and global conferences with a
view to laying out a comprehensive rights-based development agenda, including quantitative goals, timebound targets and numerical indicators.
The consensus is that goals and targets mobilise national and international partners into action and help
forge new alliances for development. They also provide a means for benchmarking and assessing
progress in development. Policy reforms, institutional change and budget reallocations often result from
discussions centred on time-bound targets. Yet, less than one-third of developing countries have set
specific and quantifiable national targets for reducing poverty.
In September 2000, 147 heads of State and Government, and 191 nations in total, adopted the Millennium
Declaration. The Declaration outlines peace, security and development concerns, including in the areas
of environment, human rights, and governance. The Declaration mainstreams a set of inter-connected
and mutually reinforcing development goals into a global agenda. The International Development Goals
(IDGs) and the development goals contained in the Millennium Declaration are similar but also, in some
respects, different, as the Millennium Declaration appears more ambitious that the IDGs. The
Declaration also contains a number of goals beyond those linked to poverty, e.g. peace and security,
environmental protection, human rights, democracy and good governance. Recently, the sets have been
merged under the designation of "Millennium Development Goals" (MDGs) as attached in Annex D.
The common list of MDGs prepared collaboratively by the UN, WB, IMF and OECD does not undercut
in any way agreements on other goals and targets reached at the world summits and global conferences
during the 1990s. The MDGs, which incorporate the IDGs, synthesize the goals and targets for
monitoring human development. They centre on eight major goals:
! Eradicate poverty and hunger
! Achieve universal primary education
! Promote gender equality and empower women
! Reduce child mortality
! Improve maternal health
! Combat HIV/AIDS, malaria and other diseasesUnited Nations Development Assistance Framework for the Lao PDR 2002-2006
15
! Ensure environmental sustainability
! Develop a global partnership for development
Numerical targets have been set for each goal. Most goals are to be achieved over a 25-year period –
between 1990-2015. Appropriate indicators have been selected to monitor progress on each of the
targets. The MDGs incorporate most of the goals and targets set at the global conferences and world
summits of the 1990s, as well as the goals contained in the Millennium Declaration. The MDGs should
be considered as indicative for country-level monitoring, not as a rigid directive. There are other goals
and targets such as those on environment set at the UNCED or on reproductive health set at the ICPD that
can also be used for monitoring human development.
MDG monitoring will take place at the global and country levels. At the global level, the UN SecretaryGeneral will report annually to the General Assembly on progress towards a sub-set of the MDGs and to
report more comprehensively every five years. These reports will support a dynamic campaign to help
keep poverty issues front and centre of the national and global development agenda. At the country level,
MDG reports (MDGRs) will help to engage the Government, civil society, communities, general public
and the media in a systematic and identifiable follow-up to the global conferences and world summits of
the 1990s. Furthermore, assistance for periodic reporting on progress towards the MDGs at the country
level will be an important contribution of the UN System to the implementation of the Millennium
Declaration, at a time when the world is expecting renewed vigour of the organization.
The CCA, PRSP and National Human Development Report processes will contribute to the preparation of
MDGR. For example, both the CCA and MDGR focus on similar national and global goals, targets and
indicators, and both aim to support the development of sustainable statistical systems and capacities to
analyse and use data for policy-making and programming. Reporting on the UNDAF implementation will
be closely linked with monitoring the progress achieved in reaching the MDGs. Thus, the present
UNDAF outlines the UN System support to the Lao PDR for achieving its national development goals in
integrity with the global MDGs and goals of the Millennium Declaration.
C. The Lao PDR’s Development Context

The Lao PDR is a ‘Least Developed Country’ (LDC), and as such is considered by the international
community to be one of the poorest countries in the world. Although there are signs that poverty levels
are falling, poverty remains widespread throughout the Lao PDR, with many households unable to meet

especially in northern provinces, and among ethnic groups inhabiting remote areas, the uneducated, and

The Lao PDR is a landlocked country, two thirds of which is mountainous. Geographic conditions
restrict both the quantity and quality of agricultural land and pose difficulties in the development of trade,
social infrastructure, and transport and communications links. Nevertheless, the Lao PDR is located in
the centre of a dynamic and prospering region and as such has the potential to provide a strategic resource
base and land link to its neighbours – Vietnam, Thailand, Cambodia, Myanmar and China. As part of the
reform process launched under the umbrella of the New Economic Mechanism (NEM) in 1986, the Lao
PDR has sought to strengthen international and regional ties. The Lao PDR is now a member of many
regional and international organizations, including the Mekong River Commission (MRC) and, since July
1997, a member of the Association of South-East Asian Nations (ASEAN).
Given a current population growth rate, the Lao population of about 5.1 million is expected to double in
25 years, as persons under 20 years of age, who currently comprise about 54% of the total population,
enter their reproductive years. Although fertility is falling, as more women and men adopt family
planning methods, the national fertility rate remains high. High population growth coupled with a high
age-dependency ratio and increasing population densities are placing a growing demand on agricultural
land and social services. As more adolescents enter working age, competition for scarce employment
opportunities will substantially increase in the coming decades.
The Lao PDR is an ethnically diverse country, with 47 officially recognized ethnic groups, with their own
customs and dialects. Across the country regional, lowland-upland, urban-rural, ethnic and gender
disparities are reflected in inequities in access to fertile land, basic social services, transport and
communications. The Lao Loum, who traditionally live in more fertile lowlands and prosperous urban
areas along the Mekong corridor, account for some 52.5% of the total population and represent the
majority in eight of the 18 provinces. While over 65% of the population are Buddhist, a third are animist
and the Lao PDR also has a number of religious groups, for example Christians, who constitute 1.3% of
the population.
Despite considerable improvements in the quality of life over the past two decades, the general health
status of the Lao population remains low. The health situation is characterized by low life expectancy,
high infant, under-five and maternal mortality rates. Only one half of the total population has access to
safe drinking water, and less than half to safe sanitation facilities. The health status of the population is
generally worse in remote rural areas, and among women, small ethnic groups, the poor and the
uneducated. Lao people, especially the young, are also increasingly vulnerable to HIV/AIDS and drug
addiction.
Although quantitative and qualitative progress in education has been made in recent years, a significant
proportion of children, especially girls and ethnic groups in remote areas, are not guaranteed an equal
opportunity to a basic education. Access to secondary and tertiary education is particularly limited and
just under 30% of the adult population is illiterate. Economic growth coupled with rapid population
growth is increasing the demand for education services and for vocationally qualified people. The quality
of education available, however, is currently inadequate to meet economic and social demands, even for
the few who complete it.
Although the Lao PDR has experienced significant advances in social development in recent years, the
country is categorized as having a ‘low level of human development’. In 2001, the Lao PDR was ranked
131st out of 162 countries in the UNDP Human Development Index (HDI), making it one of the poorest
countries in South-East Asia, and 119th in the UNDP Gender-related Development Index (GDI), indicating
the existence of significant gender disparities.2

services, inputs and markets, and thus lack the means to commercialize agricultural production and
generate alternatives to subsistence lifestyles.
The Lao PDR is highly dependent on natural resources for economic and social development. Economic
expansion, population growth and non-sustainable environmental practices and livelihoods are placing an
increasing strain on urban and rural environments and biodiversity. Deforestation and soil erosion are
particularly serious problems, threatening ecosystems and agricultural livelihoods. Urban population
growth coupled with increasing rural to urban migration is beginning to impact heavily on fragile urban
infrastructures, such as solid waste disposal systems, while urban environments face increasing pollution.
Natural disasters, particularly floods and droughts, pose considerable threats to long-term sustainable
development.
The Lao economy remains significantly dependent on Official Development Assistance (ODA). Exports

D. National Development Priorities and Goals
D.1. Overarching National Goal
The Lao PDR’s overarching development goal is to quit the status of LDC by the year 2020 through
sustainable and equitable development, i.e. “sustained growth with equity”. The Government intends to
achieve this major goal of eradicating mass poverty by:
• Efficient protection of environment and eco-systems, and sustainable use of natural resources;
• Increased participation of all stakeholders – regions, provinces, districts and villages – in the
development process;
• Continued implementation of the New Economic Mechanism (NEM).3
The Government adopted a harmonious ‘triangular’, mutually reinforcing approach to growth and
development, as embodied in the notion of sustained growth with equity:
D.2. Stages in National Development
Since 1975, the Government has endeavoured to continuously strengthen the stability of society and has
instituted national development policies on a ‘step by step’ basis. The basic tenet underlying the ‘step by
step’ approach is to ensure that changes are introduced gradually, and at a rate that does not make them
counterproductive or disruptive to society. The guiding principle is to preserve national values and
cultural heritage and to maintain a united society, whilst at the same time to take part in regional
integration and globalization.
The national development efforts in the Lao PDR have taken place in the context of three stages. These
stages are closely inter-linked and need to be developed simultaneously to ensure the progressive
transition from an isolated, subsistence-based rural economy to a production and services economy, as the
condition for advancing coherently towards the 2020 goal.
Stage One: Establishment and implementation of the NEM
The NEM was launched by the Government in 1986 in order to gradually transform the economy from a
centrally planned to a market oriented model through a number of key reforms, including the
liberalization of prices; introduction of trade systems and a two-tier banking sector; introduction of a
legal, regulatory and administrative framework needed to support a market economy; increased transfer of
managerial and financial autonomy to, and privatization of, State Owned Enterprises (SOEs); and
increased regional integration.

Stage Two: Structural transformation and capacity building of the economy
Since the introduction of the NEM, the Government has undertaken structural transformations designed to
promote national integration, develop a sustainable economic resource base, and build-up the basic
economic, physical and social infrastructure of the country, with a focus on the development of transport
and communications networks. The Government has also sought to promote regional integration, moving
towards becoming a full economic partner among countries in the dynamic region and shifting from being
a landlocked to a ‘landlinked’ country.
Stage Three: People-centred and sustainable development
Participatory people-centred development is central to the Government’s development efforts. At its core
this includes the achievement of basic food security, the preservation of natural resources and the
decentralization of development responsibilities to enable greater public participation. The immediate aim
is to enhance conditions everywhere in the country, enabling the multi-ethnic population to have access to
what are considered the basics of sustainable development: food security, access to markets, education
and health.
The Lao PDR is predominantly a rural society with an agriculturally based economic structure. The
improvement of social conditions and the creation of incomes, especially in rural areas, are top
Government’s priorities. The integration of rural areas into the national market economy is seen as
central to eliminating widespread poverty. Rural development, in its social and physical dimensions, is
therefore considered the key to the eradication of mass poverty and sustainable improvements in social
well-being.
D.3. Eight National Socio-Economic Priority Programmes
The eight national socio-economic priority programmes have been devised to channel the Government’s
development efforts in a focused way towards the 2020 goal. They serve as a major reference for the
national planning system, and for defining the national investment priorities. Of these priority
programmes, achieving permanent food security, preserving the country’s natural resources, and
developing the national human resource potential, are given the highest importance.
Food production – The programme aims to ensure food security by increasing food and rice production.
It promotes more intensive and diversified food production, including increasing the productivity of rice,
the expansion of dry and rainy season irrigation in identified priority plains, improved animal husbandry
and crop varieties, and more appropriate use of machinery, fertilizers, manure and pesticide.
Commercial production – The programme seeks to promote investment in commodities including coffee,
fruit and forest products, large livestock and fisheries, to encourage exports including hydropower and
mining development, to promote light and small-scale industries and handicrafts, and more varied
agricultural production. The programme promotes increased commercial production and the development
of processing industries and handicraft enterprises as a means to generate income.
Stabilization and reduction of shifting cultivation – The Government wishes to protect forests and the
environment by providing sedentary settlements, extension programmes and start-up resources for shifting
cultivators.
Rural development – The intention in this sector is to bring together rural development efforts in an
integrated and focused manner within a clearly defined geographical area. The focal sites development
strategy is designed to provide development services in an integrated and locally owned way, from the
construction of basic transport infrastructure, education and heath care facilities to skills development,
aimed at improving the living standards in rural areas. Other aims are increasing food and commercialUnited Nations Development Assistance Framework for the Lao PDR 2002-2006

production, creating employment opportunities and establishing the conditions for improved living
standards in rural areas, thereby reducing rural-urban disparities and rural to urban migration.
Infrastructure development – The programme seeks to modernize national and international
communications and transport networks, including roads, bridges, airports and river port facilities, and to
expand postal and telecommunication services in all regions, transforming Lao PDR from a landlocked to
a ‘landlinked’ sub-regional hub in ASEAN.
Improved socio-economic management and foreign economic relations – Goals are to consolidate the
NEM and reinforce conditions for the high economic growth essential for development. On the domestic
side, the programme seeks to promote domestic production and develop rural markets. On the
international side, it aims to expand international trade and reduce the external trade deficit, by increasing
the quality and quantity of export goods, lifting regulations and mechanisms hampering export-orientated
production, securing increased foreign investment, promoting transit trade, re-export and duty-free zones,
and preparing for AFTA and WTO membership.
Human resource development – The programme is designed to build capacity at the individual,
institutional and community level in nine sub-programmes: education; labour and social welfare; public
health; civil service and public administration; culture and information; Lao Women’s Union; youth; Lao
Federation of Trade Unions; and the Lao Front for National Construction. The objectives are to link
training to the Lao PDR’s socio-economic goals, to upgrade knowledge and skills, to build managerial
and technical capacities, and to enhance leadership.
Services development – The programme aims to generate increased foreign revenue, primarily through
the development of the tourism sector. The country is endeavouring to improve tourism infrastructure, to
facilitate entry into the Lao PDR by improving procedures, ports-of-entry and transit posts, to develop
tourist routes in each region, and to train personnel in the tourism sector.
D.4. National Socio-Economic Development Plans
The Government’s development efforts are captured through the 5-year national socio-economic
development plans (NSEDPs) as the principal medium-term planning instruments. All the NSEDPs are
geared to improving in a sustainable way the living conditions of the Lao PDR’s multi-ethnic population,
and to help the country achieve its 2020 goal.
The National Socio-Economic Development Plan 1996-2000 sets out the key tasks, guidelines and targets
for national development up to 2000. The objectives of the NSEDP 1996-2000 were aimed at (1) poverty
reduction, especially in rural and multi-ethnic areas; (2) infrastructure development; and (3) human
resource development. The general guidelines affirmed continued building of sectoral and regional
economic structures in conjunction with the preservation of the natural environment, regional socioeconomic development linked to the development of ethnic mountainous areas, and the gradual reduction
of the gap between urban, rural and mountainous areas.
The new National Socio-Economic Development Plan 2001-2005 provides a cohesive platform for
progress in the 21st century and progressive industrialization and modernization beyond the year 2000.
The overall goals of the NSEDP 2001-2005 are to ensure that the country enjoys firm social order and
political stability, and to generate consistent economic growth. The plan aims to reduce the incidence of
poverty to less than one half of its current rate4
; to secure adequate rice and food supply for the whole
country; to resolve the issue of slash-and-burn cultivation and eliminate opium and marijuana production

2011-2020: Economic and social development which will enable the country to quite the status of LDC.

National Poverty Reduction Strategy (NPRS), which will focus on fighting poverty through human

For the period 2001-2010, the key national development objectives include:

• To gradually improve living standards of the multi-ethnic population;
• To establish food security for the whole country and to enhance export of agricultural commodities;

D.7. National Development Goals by Region
Given the geographic and ethnic diversity of the Lao PDR, the country is divided into three main regions,
each having its unique features, specific development needs and potentials.
The North encompasses seven provinces with 30% of the population and 40% of the land area. It is
considered the most underdeveloped part of the country, characterized by poor living conditions, low
education levels, and environment damaged by deforestation. The Government’s key development goals
for the North include:
• Development of infrastructure, in particular the communications network;
• Preservation of forest resources, and reforestation;
• Stabilization of shifting cultivation, and elimination of opium poppy and combating other drugs;
• Ensuring household food security;
• Promotion of commercial production (cash crops, animal husbandry etc.);
• Tourism development; and
• Establishment of a special economic area in Oudomxay province, a duty-free trade area in Boten,
Luang Namtha province, and the pentagon economic area in the northern region.
The Centre encompasses seven provinces with 46% of the population and 40% of the land area. It is the
most developed region of the Lao PDR, possessing vast potentials for further development, particularly in
the field of agriculture and hydro-electricity. Key development goals for the Centre are:
• Infrastructure development;
• Development of hydro-electricity, agriculture and forestry, production of construction materials,
utilities and export goods;
• Development of trade, tourism and transit transport systems; and
• Establishment of a special economic area in Savannakhet province.
The South encompasses 4 provinces with 24% of the population and 18% of the land area. It is a very
important strategic region, bordered by Vietnam, Cambodia and Thailand, with enormous potentials for
development of forestry, agriculture, hydro-electricity and mining. The Government established the
following key development goals for the South:
• Development of infrastructure, turning the region into a transit route;
• Expansion of commercial crops and fruit trees, promotion of cattle rearing, and manufacture of export
products based on agriculture (mainly coffee, cardamom and rice);
• Development of agro-processing industry and mining;
• Development of trade, tourism and handicrafts; and
• Establishment of a special economic area in Champassak province and the triangle economic area in
Attapeu province.

improving the livelihoods in a sustainable and equitable manner.
• Capacity and institutional building and human resource development;
• Reducing disparities in income distribution; and
• Reducing the gap between rural and urban areas.
The external challenges reflect the Lao PDR’s determination to become an active participant in the region

(3) Strategic support priorities: governance and public administration reform including decentralization,

D.9. Strategic Approach to Poverty Eradication
As a result of the 2000 Participatory Poverty Assessment and the subsequent Interim Poverty Reduction
Strategy Paper (I-PRSP) preparation process, the Government established a coherent strategic approach to
poverty alleviation by identifying the main sectors, which at the current stage are expected to contribute
most decisively to poverty reduction. These four sectors are (1) agriculture, forestry, livestock and
fisheries; (2) education; (3) health; and (4) road infrastructure. Whilst development and improvement in
all sectors of the economy are needed to achieve sustainable long-term development, the four sectors
represent the backbone of the Government’s approach to immediate poverty alleviation.
The Government undertook a major effort for establishing national long-term strategic visions for these
sectors, by holding seven policy dialogues with the donor community during 2000, as part of the Round
Table process.5
 Action plans will concretize the strategic visions into operational programmes and
projects, which in turn will be integrated into the Public Investment Plan (PIP).
From key investments in the four main sectors, coupled with the improved governance and sound macroeconomic policies, the Government expects a number of direct and/or combined outputs, including:
• Food security;
• Improved human resource base and effective people’s participation;
• National integration (reducing the regional and rural-urban income gaps through equal distribution of
resources and a wider access to public goods and services); and
• Sustainable social progress guaranteeing quality health care, protection and participation rights of
children and women, quality education and other social services to every member of the society.

D.10. Towards Better Governance
The Government considers governance as a key inter-sectoral element to achieve economic growth and
poverty reduction, and as an essential condition for graduating from the LDC’s status by the year 2020.
It has thus placed great emphasis on a Governance and Public Administration Reform (GPAR)
programme.
The Government defines good governance as an incremental process aiming for the best possible state of
institutional and structural arrangements, decision-making processes, policy formulation, implementation
and coordination capacity, information flows, leadership and relationships between the Government and
people. The key cornerstones of the GPAR programme are:
• Public sector management improvement;
• Sound financial management;
• Effective public service personnel management;
• Judicial/ legal reform;
• Implementation of the Government’s decentralization policy6
;
• Local governance reform initiatives; and
• Human resource development.
Over the long term, the Government expects from its GPAR programme: sounder governance, improved
service delivery, better support for market economy, more cost effective running of local administration,
improved accountability and control, and improved overall credibility of Government.

E. A United Nations Response to the Lao PDR’s Development Needs and
Priorities
Since 1957, the United Nations has assisted the Lao PDR in achieving a diverse programme of socioeconomic goals through a country-led process. During these years, the UN has accumulated considerable
country knowledge and expertise and has developed a trusted partnership with the Government and people
of the Lao PDR. The UN continues to be in an important position to deliver the wealth of its universal
experience through an impartial, cross-sectoral and people-centred approach to development assistance.
The UN relies on its multi-cultural character and convening power to bring to the Lao PDR the examples
of best international practices and modern technical expertise.
While UN assistance currently represents a comparatively modest proportion of the total Official
Development Assistance (ODA) to the country, the UN support remains significant in its form of grant
aid. Through such impartial aid, and the unparalleled breadth of development knowledge, the UN will
continue to play a catalytic role in the national policy dialogue, and to advocate for the Global Agenda for
Development. The close relationship between the UN System and the Government is also pivotal in
bringing forth participatory development projects that aim to build long-term sustainability and national
ownership.
At the same time, the UN places a high importance on building and advancing meaningful partnerships
with the Bretton Woods Institutions7
, the Asian Development Bank, key bilateral donors, nongovernmental and civil society organizations, and the emerging private sector, all being essential players
in the national development process.
Overarching Goal of the United Nations in the Lao PDR
The overarching goal of the UN assistance in the Lao PDR in the next programme cycle (2002-2006) is to
provide support to the national development needs and priorities, and promote the implementation of
the declarations and programmes of action of the world conferences and international conventions,
including the human rights instruments, to which the Lao PDR is a State party. In doing so, the UN
will pursue the four major goals: development and poverty eradication policies and strategies; response to
basic human needs; sustainable use of natural resources and preservation of cultural heritage; and human
rights, gender equality and good governance, using multi-sectoral and inter-agency approaches.
Development and poverty eradication policies and strategies – The Government of the Lao PDR has
adopted the overarching goal of freeing the country from underdevelopment and quitting the status of
LDC by the year 2020, as the major commitment of the World Summit for Social Development, 1995.
The eradication of mass poverty in the Lao PDR is, therefore, the underlying objective of the Government
and UN System development efforts. The UN in close partnership with the BWIs and ADB will provide
support to the formulation and implementation of fully integrated and coordinated poverty reduction
strategies and programmes, including the Full PRSP, Participatory Poverty Assessment, Vulnerability
Analysis Mapping (VAM), and National Human Development Report, all in close cooperation with the
CPC and NSC. Comprehensive and well designed policies and strategies for development and poverty
eradication are requisite for the provision of adequate response to basic human needs, sustainable use of
natural resources and preservation of cultural heritage, as well as the promotion of human rights and good
governance.

III. Goals and Objectives of the United Nations in the Lao PDR
2002-2006
This chapter outlines the main goals and objectives of the United Nations in partnership with the Bretton
Woods Institutions and Asian Development Bank in the Lao PDR over the next five years, in response to
the key development issues and challenges identified in the first Common Country Assessment 2000. At
the same time, each of the UNDAF goals supports the national development priorities and goals outlined
in the National Socio-Economic Development Plans and Strategies to 2005, 2010 and 2020, 7th Round
Table Meeting strategies, Interim Poverty Reduction Strategy Paper, and other key policy and strategy
documents of the Government; as well as supports the attainment of the relevant Millennium Declaration
Goals (attached in Annex E).
Indeed, the UNDAF Lao PDR reflects the larger Millennium Declaration Goals, which not only fully
incorporate all of the Millennium Development Goals, but extend further to include other important goals
(such as peace, security and disarmament – in particular eliminating UXO and drugs, development and
poverty eradication, protecting our common environment, human rights, democracy and good
governance, and protecting the vulnerable).
For the specific interventions, UN agency, Government and donor partners, and cooperation strategies
under each of these goals, please refer to the “UNDAF Lao PDR Matrix” attached as Annex A.
A. Development and Poverty Eradication Policies and Strategies
Millennium Declaration Goals
We will spare no effort to free our fellow man, women and children from the abject and dehumanizing
conditions of extreme poverty, to which more than a billion of them are currently subjected. We are
committed to making the right to development a reality for everyone and to freeing the entire human race
from want.
National development goals
Overarching goal – The Lao PDR aims to quit once and for all the status of a LDC by the year 2020
through a sustainable and equitable development. The Lao Government’s fundamental commitment to a
sustained growth with equity calls for a direct attack on poverty. Quitting the LDC status, for the Lao
PDR, essentially means eradicating mass poverty, and also eliminating inequalities and improving the
people’s living standards. This implies two major strategies: high economic growth with equity and
access to social services and markets for everybody, particularly those in the rural areas.8
Regionalization, internationalization and globalization – Active membership in ASEAN and AFTA will
enable the Lao PDR to strengthen its role as a land-link at the centre of the GMS. The membership in
ASEAN and AFTA also entails the need to produce goods and services on a competitive basis to
encourage joint venture projects and to promote the economic sectors in which the Lao PDR has
comparative advantages. Increased national/regional development interface through regional cooperation
schemes (in particular GMS and West-East corridor programmes) will help to narrow the gap between the
Lao PDR and other countries of the region. Joining the WTO is a logical continuation of the open-door
policy as reflected by the Lao PDR’s adhesion to ASEAN-AFTA. The Lao PDR believes in the
globalization process since it considers that it will help to achieve the overarching goal of alleviating
poverty and to create a more prosperous and peaceful society.

ICT – The Government recognizes the importance of bridging the technology gap, or “digital divide”.
Information production and management technology complements the challenges related to human
resource development and capacity building. Bridging these gaps will strengthen the fundamentals of the
Lao economy, to progressively overcome the lack of expertise hindering national development.9
Macroeconomic priorities – The Government’s approach to macroeconomic management supports the
objectives and targets of the socio-economic development plan in relation to stabilization (controlling the
inflation and maintaining the value of the Kip), growth (achieving a growth rate of 7% by 2003),
implementation of the budget and investment plans, and enhancement of the decentralization process.
These are also the key priorities for poverty alleviation. Low inflation, i.e. price stability, is a basic
requirement to improve the situation of the poor, as are fiscal stability to ensure a continuous support to
pro-poor investments, and a well-functioning financial sector to enhance access to credit, income
generating activities, increased market production and improved social services.10
A.1. Facing up to Regionalization, Internationalization and Globalization
Millennium Declaration/Development Goals
We believe that the central challenge we face today is to ensure that globalization becomes a positive
force for all the world’s people.
We undertake to address the special needs of the Least Developed Countries. We call on the
industrialized countries:
♦ To adopt a policy of duty- and quota-free access for essentially all exports from the Least Developed
Countries; and
♦ To implement the enhanced programme of debt relief for the heavily indebted poor countries without
further delay and to agree to cancel all official bilateral debts of those countries in return for their
making demonstrable commitments to poverty reduction.
We recognize the special needs and problems of the landlocked developing countries, and urge both
bilateral and multilateral donors to increase financial and technical assistance to this group of countries
to meet their special development needs and to help them overcome the impediments of geography by
improving their transit transport systems.
We also resolve to ensure that the benefits of new technologies, especially information and
communications technologies, are available to all.
Key challenges
The Lao PDR is situated in the centre of a dynamic and prosperous region. As a full member of ASEAN,
the Lao PDR is strategically placed to capitalize on regional growth and transform itself from a
‘landlocked’ to a ‘landlinked’ country. It is essential that the Lao PDR continues to deepen external
socio-economic engagement, strengthen international trade ties and partnerships, and develop international
infrastructure networks, including transport, communications and information technology links. Unless
the Lao PDR fully embraces regional and global opportunities, it risks falling behind its neighbours and
becoming marginalized.
UNDAF support
The UN System in partnership with the BWIs and ADB is committed to supporting the Lao PDR regional
integration and transformation to a ‘landlinked’ country through its active participation in ASEAN and
MRC, and the development of important economic and social linkages through the Greater Mekong Sub-

region programme. The UN Country Team will assist the Government in completing formalities required
for accession to the WTO, and building sufficient capacity to enable meaningful participation in regional
and international forums. In addition, the UN programmes will aim at promoting the use of media
networks and Internet, and developing a national ICT access and strategy framework.
A.2. Developing a Comprehensive National Policy Environment
Millennium Declaration Goals
We resolve to create an environment – at the national and global levels alike – which is conducive to
development and to the elimination of poverty.
Key challenges
In order for the Lao PDR to fully meet its national development aspirations, it is essential to ensure the
development of clear, inclusive, coordinated, effective and sustainable Government policies and
strategies. National development priorities need to be comprehensively and clearly articulated, and to
remain responsive to changes in national, regional and international economic and socio-political
environments.
UNDAF support
The UN Country Team will provide support to the Government in its effort to develop, implement and
monitor a comprehensive set of national policies, strategies and guidelines, articulating the national
development priorities in a wide range of areas: from forestry and fisheries, industry and handicraft
development, electricity and mining management, microfinance, to education, health, reproductive health,
HIV/AIDS prevention and opium elimination. For effective implementation of these strategies, the UN
will facilitate cross-sectoral coordination between the Government, donors and private sector.
A.3. Developing and Maintaining an Enabling Macroeconomic Environment, and
Strengthening and Deepening the Reform Process
Millennium Declaration/Development Goals
Success, in meeting the objectives of development and poverty elimination depends, inter alia, on good
governance within each country. It also depends on good governance at the international level and on
transparency in the financial, monetary and trading systems. We are committed to an open, equitable,
rule-based, predictable and non-discriminatory multilateral trading and financial system.
We are also determined to deal comprehensively and effectively with the debt problems of low- and
middle-income developing countries, through various national and international measures designed to
make their debt sustainable in the long term.
Key challenges
Sustainable human development cannot take place without strong, sustainable and equitable
macroeconomic progress. For the Lao PDR to quit the LDC status and reduce widespread poverty by
2020, it is essential to maintain a stable and enabling macroeconomic environment. The economy should
be conducive to private enterprise and entrepreneurial development and resistant to external shocks, such
as those witnessed during the recent Asian economic crisis.
In order to complete the necessary transformation from a command economy to a market-orientated
economy, it is essential to strengthen and deepen the reform process and maintain the momentum of
reforms introduced under the umbrella of the NEM. In particular, there is a need to continue marketbased reforms in order to strengthen macro-economic management, ensure a sustainable platform for
economic growth, and create an enabling environment for the development of a dynamic private sector.
There is also a need to continue legal-based reforms in order to strengthen the legal framework and rule
of law, with regard to law making, law enforcement and judicial processes.United Nations Development Assistance Framework for the Lao PDR 2002-2006
32
It is essential that a schedule for fundamental reforms is explicitly outlined to enable the Government,
development assistance partners, private sector and general populace to prepare for the needed changes,
minimize related risks and capitalize fully on new opportunities.
UNDAF support
The UN Country Team led by the BWIs and ADB will contribute to the overall goal of developing and
maintaining an enabling macroeconomic environment through concerted measures towards strengthening
of macroeconomic stabilization, restructuring of SOCBs, development of enterprise sector, and
encouragement of private sector development, as well as trade liberalization. Such measures will include,
among others, improving revenue collection mechanisms, maintaining monetary discipline, promoting
greater transparency and accountability in decision-making, and strengthening public expenditure
management and control functions. With the objective of fostering the development of a dynamic,
outward-looking private sector that will enable increases in per capita income and a reduction in poverty
incidence, the UN, BWIs and ADB will support key structural reforms for enhancing private sector
activity and investment.
National development goals
Reform process – In its Macroeconomic Policy and Reform Framework document prepared as part of the
Round Table process, the Government identified a series of priority reform areas:
• The monetary and exchange rate policies;
• The financial sector reform, including state-owned commercial banks, regulatory reform and rural
finance;
• The fiscal policies, including tax policies, expenditure management and public savings;
• The trade policies, including customs administration, export promotion and regulatory framework;
• The restructuring of state-owned enterprises; and
• The legal and regulatory framework with regard to promotion of all economic sectors, including
domestic and foreign private investment, strengthening of implementation and dissemination of laws,
regulations and legal information.
As part of key structural reforms, the Government intends to promote the private sector by removing
barriers to entry and leveling competition with the state sector.11
PIP and investment requirements – To secure the achievement of the NSEDP 2001-2005 targets, efforts

The PIP is the most important component of ODA, but it does not account for all technical assistance or

A.4. Strengthening Aid Coordination and Reducing Aid Dependency
Millennium Declaration/Development Goals
We call on the industrialized countries to grant more generous development assistance, especially to
countries that are genuinely making an effort to apply their resources to poverty reduction.
We recognize the special needs and problems of the landlocked developing countries, and urge both
bilateral and multilateral donors to increase financial and technical assistance to this group of countries.
Key challenges
The Lao PDR is heavily dependent on ODA for financing public investment and for providing necessary
technical inputs into development activities. In the immediate term it is essential that external aid is
effectively coordinated and managed, and maximized to its full potential and efficient use. In the medium
to long term it is essential to ensure sustainable economic growth, develop an enabling environment for
the private sector and undertake financial reforms. It is also imperative that revenue collection issues are
addressed, in order to reduce dependency on aid, to improve budgetary processes, and to ensure national
ownership of development activities.
UNDAF support
The UN System, BWIs and ADB will aim at strengthening the Government’s aid management and
coordination capacities, to ensure effective monitoring of and timely reporting on donor contributions, and
matching of donor assistance with ongoing investment projects and medium-term national priorities,
including those geared towards poverty reduction. The UN Country Team will continue to play a
catalytic role in encouraging a constructive aid dialogue between the Government and all development
assistance partners within the context of the extended Round Table Mechanism. In addition, the UN will
facilitate donor coordination in the areas of cross-cutting concern: response to natural disasters, clearance
of UXO, HIV/AIDS prevention etc.

A.5. Ensuring Adequate Resource Allocation and Sustainable Financing for Social and

Millennium Declaration Goals
We are concerned about the obstacles developing countries face in mobilizing the resources needed to

Key challenges
Although the Government of the Lao PDR is committed to the 20/20 initiative14, only around 13% of

Increased public and ODA expenditure on social services and safety nets is required to meet the growing
demand for basic services, to ensure the daily well-being of communities, households and individuals, and
to provide the ‘social capital’ necessary for national development. It is also essential to ensure that such

The Government is strongly committed to devoting at least 20% of public expenditure to the social

fostering a consensus on national needs and priorities with a particular emphasis on social and human
development, and promoting social security and cost-recovery schemes.
A.6. Addressing the Imbalance in Capital and Current Expenditure
Key challenges
Due to the infrastructure development needs receiving much emphasis, an imbalance has developed in
public investment, favouring capital expenditure over recurrent expenditure. Public budget allocations for
current expenditures, such as human resource development, salaries and the maintenance of capital
investments, are inadequate. In order to provide adequate social services in the long-term, and to ensure
the sustainability of the capital investments made, it is essential to address this disparity and the
insufficient planning for future recurrent costs.
UNDAF support
The existing imbalance in capital and current expenditure will be jointly addressed by the IMF, WB and
ADB through their support to improve budget preparation, execution, expenditure control and treasury
operations, all aimed at ensuring greater efficiency in public investment planning and recurrent
expenditure management.

Programmes

We resolve to create an environment – at the national and global levels alike – which is conducive to
development and to the elimination of poverty.

B. Response to Basic Human Needs

We are committed to making the right to development a reality for everyone and to freeing the entire

National development goals
Sectoral priorities – The main dimensions of the Government’s strategic approach to poverty alleviation
are the four fundamental sectors, namely agriculture and forestry, education, health, and road
infrastructure. Sound macro-economic management, including economic stability, fiscal, financial, as
well as legal and regulatory reforms, together with decentralization and participation are fundamental
trans-sectoral conditions necessary to ensure successful implementation of the sectoral priorities.

preoccupations. Investments in irrigation facilities, farm-to-market roads and improved access to social

forestry development is most conspicuously embodied in the Government’s rural development priorities.
The agricultural policy supports the farmers’ livelihood approaches, which aim at achieving household

B.1. Developing Sustainable Livelihoods and Ensuring Household Food Security
Millennium Declaration/Development Goals
To halve, between 1990 and 2015, the proportion of people who suffer from hunger.
Key challenges
Access to a stable, safe and nutritionally adequate food supply underpins the basic health needs of all
people and is essential for ensuring a healthy standard of living and productive life. The vast majority of
households in the Lao PDR, particularly in remote areas, remain dependent on subsistence agriculture,
and many households face regular food deficits, deficiencies in daily food intake and/or chronic and acute
malnutrition. Encouraging agricultural commercialization and the development of agricultural
infrastructure, such as irrigation schemes and agricultural extension systems, can transform agricultural
activities from subsistence to surplus. Assisting in the development of sustainable livelihoods will ensure
continual household access to a safe and nutritious food supply as well as other basic household needs. It
is also important to generate diversified and alternative sources of income and raise wage labour incomes
in both urban and rural areas.
UNDAF support
Ensuring household food security through increased food and rice production is one of the Government’s
eight priority programmes, supported by the UN System, WB and ADB. The UN and its partners will
aim at promoting adequate and long-term funding and capacity building for the development of
agriculture, agricultural extension, livestock and fisheries, and agro-processing. At the policy level, the
UN Country Team will assist in the formulation of policies and strategies to promote sustainable,
intensified and diversified food production, encouraging small-scale and participatory development
schemes. WFP will coordinate inter-agency support to community identified and prioritized schemes
using labour based approach with food-for-work directed to the most vulnerable and food insecure areas.
The emphasis will also be placed on enabling the effective disaster prevention and management systems,
to strengthen household preparedness and coping abilities, and to establish a national strategic food
reserve.
In the area of nutrition, the UN will provide support to increasing awareness of nutrition among decisionmakers, and strengthening institutional capacity and coordination in the overall context of national
planning and health sector reform. Specific UN interventions will be targeted towards the reduced
incidence of malnutrition, elimination of vitamin A deficiency and Iodine Deficiency Disorder, promotion
of breast-feeding, and improved family nutrition practices.

B.2. Meeting Basic Household Needs
Millennium Declaration/Development Goals
By the year 2015, to halve the proportion of people who are unable to reach or to afford safe drinking
water.
By 2020, to have achieved a significant improvement in the lives of at least 100 million slum dwellers.
Key challenges
Despite large investments in infrastructure, many Lao households still lack access to basic household
amenities. There is a shortfall in the inputs essential for developing and maintaining sustainable incomes,
including irrigation facilities, credit and extension services, markets and market information. Lack of
access, particularly for the rural population, derives from the limited physical infrastructure and
communications networks (particularly roads), low levels of income and therefore affordability, and low
levels of the education and information that empowers people to make informed choices. Improving
physical, financial and knowledge based access is essential for improving social conditions and living
standards, and enhancing and expanding economic opportunities. Unless difficulties in access are
adequately addressed, a large segment of the Lao population will remain isolated and unable to participate
in society or meaningfully contribute to national development.
UNDAF support
The UN Country Team will support the Government’s efforts towards improving access of Lao
population to basic household utilities, through labour based and locally owned construction of rural
access roads, irrigation facilities, and electrification. An important objective will be to strengthen access,
use and sustainability (financial and operational) of new and existing water supply and sanitation facilities,
ensuring equitable access for the poor, all ethnic groups, urban and rural areas. Centrally located water
supply systems will reduce the workload of women and children. The UN development programmes will
also contribute to improved health and hygiene education for the maximized health and socio-economic
impact of safe water and sanitation. A particular consideration will be given to assessing environmental
and social impacts, and enhancing monitoring mechanisms for the road sector development, and
implementation of water and sanitation schemes. In addition, the UN will support the development of
sustainable microfinance and microcredit services, income generating activities, vocational and life skills.
B.3. Ensuring Equal Access to Basic Education of Good Quality with a Special Focus on
Girls Education
Millennium Declaration/Development Goals
To ensure that, by the year 2015, children everywhere, boys and girls alike, will be able to complete a full
course of primary schooling.
To eliminate gender disparity in primary and secondary education preferably by 2005, and to all levels of
education no later than 2015.
Key challenges
Many Lao households still lack access to basic social services, including education, health and
reproductive health care. Many people seek medical attention too late, while over a fifth of children of
primary school age are not enrolled in education. Lack of access, particularly for the rural population,
derives not only from the limited physical infrastructure and low incomes, but also from the low levels of
the education and information that empowers people to make informed choices.
The achievement of quality, efficiency, access and equity in education in the Lao PDR is constrained by
such factors as high demographic growth, ethnic and cultural diversity of the population, insufficientUnited Nations Development Assistance Framework for the Lao PDR 2002-2006
