transport infrastructure, limited financial and human resources, and low institutional capacity. Despite
the steady improvements in education in the last decade, high incidence of non- and over age enrolment,
high repetition and drop out, and low completion rates persist. Many children, especially girls and ethnic
groups inhabiting remote areas, do not enjoy equal access to a basic education. Access to secondary and
tertiary education is also limited and a significant number of adults remain illiterate. The country’s
development places an increasing demand for educated and vocationally qualified people, able to
meaningfully contribute to the Lao society and economy.
UNDAF support
Adequate – physical, financial and knowledge-based – access to basic social services is essential for
improving social conditions and living standards, and empowering people to exercise their basic rights as
human beings and fully contribute to national development. The UN System in collaboration with WB
and ADB is committed to supporting the Government’s objective of increasing public, donor and private
sector financing of education and health.
In the area of education, more specific objectives are: to improve both quality and availability of
education facilities, textbooks and teaching materials, particularly in remote areas; to improve the national
curriculum; to train teachers in multi-grade teaching techniques; to promote continuous cluster-based
training for school managers and teachers; and to strengthen overall planning, management and
supervision mechanisms. In all its education initiatives and interventions, the UN Country Team will
ensure a continued special focus on girls education. Attention will be given to non-formal education
(functional literacy courses and skills training tailored to village needs) and distance basic education. In
addition to basic education assistance that addresses the needs of ethnic groups, ADB is providing support
for post-secondary education and recently approved a project to improve the quality of education service
delivery at the primary and lower secondary levels.
B.4. Promoting Sound Population Development (Reproductive Health)
Key challenges
Although the Lao PDR has a population of just over five million, with a low population density, rapid
population growth coupled with a high age-dependency ratio is placing an increasing demand on
agricultural land and basic social services. High migration and urbanization rates are also exacerbating
local planning deficiencies and placing stress on fragile urban infrastructures. It is therefore essential to
promote sound population and reproductive health policies.
Confronting the population challenges, the Lao Government elaborated a National Population and
Development Policy (NPDP) in 1999 and a 20-year cross-sector policy implementation action plan to
guide efforts for improvement in line with international programmes. The NPDP’s key objective is to
enable couples to reasonable and responsibly determine the number and spacing of children, taking into
account their own social and economic conditions, with a view to improving the quality of life and
ensuring that the country’s population growth is compatible with the socio-economic development pace.
The action plan provides a clear framework in which to target donor support in order to help families
break out of a cycle of poverty and to effect improvements in the quality of life, particularly for women
and children.
Millennium Declaration/Development Goals
Between 1990 and 2015, to have reduced maternal mortality by three quarters, and under-five child
mortality by two thirds.
UNDAF support
The UN Country Team led by UNFPA is committed to promoting sound population and development
policies. More specifically, the UN will assist the Government in the implementation of the NPDP and
action plan, as well as the associated health and education sector policies, strategies and guidelines. TheUnited Nations Development Assistance Framework for the Lao PDR 2002-2006
39
UN will target its interventions and advocacy initiatives in the area of reproductive health and gender to
advance the goals and action plan of the ICPD. Improving quality and availability of reproductive health
and family planning services particularly responsive to the needs of rural ethnic women, adolescents and
young adults, is the immediate objective.
National development goals
Reproductive health – Efforts will be made to improve the reproductive health services, in particular
family planning, and to prevent sexually transmitted infections and HIV/AIDS through the promotion of
primary health care in the whole country. By 2005, the life expectancy at birth must be at least 63 years,
maternal mortality must be less than 350 per 100,000 live births, infant mortality less than 62 per 1,000
live births, under 5 mortality 70 per 1,000 live births, and immunization rate must increase to 80%.21
HIV/AIDS prevention – The national HIV/AIDS/STI Control Programme emphasizes responses be put in
place to prevent further transmission of HIV and to minimise the negative social and economic
consequences of the HIV/AIDS epidemic for families, communities, provinces and ultimately for the
whole country, through the provision of basic information and education programmes, and safe blood
supply.
Drug control – Opium production is both a symptom and a cause of poverty. It lies at the heart of the
widespread poverty in the northern region, which is the least well-off in the country in terms of life
expectancy, education and gross domestic product. The Government is strongly determined to end the
production of opium once and for all as a basic requirement for breaking the poverty circle in the North.
The goal of the national drug control programme is to effectively eliminate the need to produce and use
opium in the Lao PDR by eradicating opium poppy cultivation by the year 2006 through an accelerated
rural development programme in the major opium producing districts. The 7th Party Congress in March
2001 reduced the allocated timeframe to 2005.
UXO clearance – The Government of the Lao PDR recognizes the urgent need to continue the UXO
decontamination in a coordinated and effective manner, focusing on one hand on clearing the land and
inhabited areas from ordnance, and on the other hand on mounting community awareness to limit the
number of accidents.22
B.5. Improving Health Status of the Population
Millennium Declaration/Development Goals
To have, by the year 2015, halted, and begun to reverse, the scourge of malaria and other major diseases
that afflict humanity.
We also resolve to encourage the pharmaceutical industry to make essential drugs more widely available
and affordable by all who need them in developing countries.
Key challenges
Despite considerable advances in the provision and utilization of health care services in recent years, the
Lao PDR is characterized by low life expectancy, high infant, under-five, childhood and maternal
mortality, and lack of access to basic health care services and facilities. Communicable diseases,
particularly malaria, ARIs, diarrhoea, and epidemics such as measles, are the major causes of child
mortality and morbidity. The incidence of these diseases is heavily influenced by a lack of education,
inadequate nutrition, lack of clean water, poor sanitation and housing conditions, and limited access to
and untimely utilisation of health care. The structure and administration of the public health care system

impede social, human and economic development, and contribute significantly to widespread poverty.
For development targets to be met, the health status of the Lao population of all ethnic groups must be

UNDAF support
The UN System, WB and ADB are committed to assist the Government in taking concerted measures

the health sector by raising Government and donor contributions and introducing social marketing and

focus on prevention initiatives, in order to increase access to health facilities and care, including
contraceptive methods, antenatal and emergency obstetric care and treatment, and rehabilitation of
substance abusers. To tackle the major causes of morbidity and mortality in the Lao PDR, the UN will
aim at strengthening the communicable disease surveillance and control systems.
B.6. Preventing an HIV/AIDS Epidemic
Millennium Declaration/Development Goals
To have, by the year 2015, halted and begun to reverse, the spread of HIV/AIDS.
To provide special assistance to children orphaned by HIV/AIDS.
Key challenges
Although the HIV/AIDS prevalence rate for persons aged 15-49 years is low at around 0.01%, the rate of
HIV/AIDS infection rate is increasing. Moreover, current statistics are almost certainly underrepresentative of the true extent of the problem, as surveillance has been limited. However, national
surveillance system was recently established to collect more reliable and systematic information on
HIV/AIDS/STIs. Changes in economic and social conditions and high HIV/AIDS prevalence rate in the
sub-region are leading to increased risk behaviour and vulnerability to HIV/AIDS infection. Unless
effective preventive action is taken to minimize the spread of HIV/AIDS, there is a high chance that the
Lao PDR could experience a serious HIV/AIDS epidemic in coming years. It is therefore essential to
increase awareness of HIV/AIDS, to strengthen multi-sectoral responses to it, and to take measures to
keep prevalence rate low.
UNDAF support
Preventing an HIV/AIDS epidemic that threatens every member of the society and increases pressure on
social services, is a cross- and multi-sectoral concern of the Government, UN System and development
assistance partners. UNAIDS inter-agency programme was launched in 1996 to assist in the coordination
of a joint response to the epidemic. The UN support will be provided to ensure clear and integrated
national HIV/AIDS responses aimed at preventing the spread of HIV infection and minimizing its socioeconomic impact. The UN Country Team is committed to assist the Government in mobilizing sufficient
internal and external resources for HIV/AIDS prevention; building HIV/AIDS institutional and
administrative framework; and extending adequate HIV/AIDS/STI counseling, testing, care and support
services to affected population. An important objective is to enhance HIV/AIDS education and awareness
that will lead to safer behaviour, especially among adolescents, young women and other vulnerable
groups.United Nations Development Assistance Framework for the Lao PDR 2002-2006
41
B.7. Eliminating Opium Production, Drug Abuse and Drug Trafficking
Millennium Declaration Goals
To redouble our efforts to implement our commitment to counter the world drug problem.
Key challenges
The Lao PDR is among the largest opium producers in the world and has the second highest rate of opiate
abuse worldwide. Opium is used by ethnic groups in remote highlands to generate cash income for food
and other basic household necessities, to sustain opium addiction prevalent in opium producing areas and
as a medicine in the absence of health services. The elimination of poverty, which is especially high in
opium producing areas, is closely tied to the elimination of opium production and the reduction of opium
abuse. Therefore, integrated rural development plans aimed at eliminating opium production and abuse
are vital.
UNDAF support
Highlighting a strong political will of the Government to end the production of opium in the Lao PDR,
the Prime Minister’s Order No. 14 of November 2000 commanded the provinces to set opium eradication
goals that will result in the crop’s total elimination by 2006. The UN Country Team led by UNDCP is
committed to supporting the Government’s balanced approach to poverty alleviation and opium
elimination, composed of three main elements: alternative development, community-based drug demand
reduction, and law enforcement. Alternative development aims to replace the illicit crop with alternative
income sources and social services. Community-based drug demand reduction brings a particular focus to
the drug aspects of health and economic well-being of individuals and families impacted by drug abuse.
Law enforcement is a key means to stop illicit trafficking at both national and regional levels. The UN
Country Team will also provide policy support for provincial adaptation to the National Strategy for
Opium Elimination, and the National Drug Demand Reduction Strategy. More specific objectives address
the prevention and awareness raising of ATS among high risks groups (including young people), and
opium and ATS addicts detoxification and rehabilitation.
B.8. Removing Unexploded Ordnance (UXO) Contamination
Millennium Declaration Goals
We will spare no effort to free our peoples from the scourge of war, whether within or between states,
which has claimed more than 5 million lives in the past decade. We will also seek to eliminate the
dangers posed by weapons of mass destruction.
Key challenges
Rural development in the Lao PDR is severely hampered by UXO contamination. Some 50% of the Lao
PDR’s land surface, and fifteen of eighteen provinces, are contaminated with UXO. The widespread
presence of UXO in many rural areas has been responsible for more than 10,000 accidents since 1975,
and continues to constraint poverty reduction efforts, threaten people’s lives, impede food production and
infrastructure construction. Work must continue to systematically clear UXO, prevent UXO related
accidents, and ensure that rural development activities take full account of UXO related issues.
UNDAF support
Removing UXO contamination is an important objective of the Government, UN System, bilateral donors
and NGOs. The UN will provide administrative and financial support to the UXO Trust Fund, mobilizing
resources for development and implementation of the Lao National Programme for UXO Clearance and
Awareness (UXO LAO). Specific objectives include: to fully integrate UXO planning with provincial
planning to offset the high cost of UXO clearance and limited availability of clearance services; to
reinforce the need for UXO planning at early stages of project development; as well as to raise
community awareness of UXO through education and mass media campaigns.United Nations Development Assistance Framework for the Lao PDR 2002-2006
42
C. Sustainable Use of Natural Resources and Preservation of Cultural
Heritage
Millennium Declaration/Development Goals
We must spare no effort to free all of humanity, and above all our children and grandchildren, from the
threat of living on a planet irredeemably spoilt by human activities, and whose resources would no longer
be sufficient for their needs.
We reaffirm our support for the principles of sustainable development, including those set out in Agenda
21, agreed upon at the United Nations Conference on Environment and Development.
We resolve therefore to adopt in all our environmental actions a new ethic of conservation and
stewardship and, at first steps, we resolve:
♦ To make every effort to ensure the entry into force of the Kyoto Protocol and to embark on the
required reduction in emission of greenhouse gases;
♦ To intensify our collective efforts for the management, conservation and sustainable development of all
types of forests;
♦ To press for the full implementation of the Convention on Biological Diversity and the Convention to
Combat Desertification;
♦ To stop the unsustainable exploitation of water resources by developing water management strategies
at the regional, national and local levels, which promote both equitable access and adequate supplies.
♦ To intensify cooperation to reduce the number and effects of natural and man-made disasters.
In a summary, to integrate the principles of sustainable development into country policies and
programmes and reverse the loss of environmental resources.
National development goals
Preserving the Lao PDR’s natural resources, especially forest and water resources, and using them in the
most sustainable way, is an integral part of the Government’s strategy to achieve sustainable and equitable
economic growth. The challenge is to balance the need for economic progress with the need to preserve
and maintain the environment in order to achieve ecologically sustainable development. Conservation of
the country’s natural resources depends on the successful implementation of an appropriate institutional
and policy framework, while optimizing revenue generation and improving livelihoods of the rural
population.23
Protecting forests – Reforestation and preservation of water source’s forests and management of national
protected forests will receive special attention. Deforestation caused by both shifting cultivation and
unsound logging practices, is leading to increased erosion and threatens the country’s natural biodiversity
and catchment areas. Efforts should be made to increase the forest cover from 47% presently to 50% by
2010.24
Preserving cultural heritage – The Government will carry out projects for preservation and development
of national historical and archaeological sites, particularly Vat Phou in Champassak, the Plane of Jars in
Xieng Khouang, Viengxay historical town; and continue to survey and prepare inventories of relics and
places of historical, scientific and cultural value with a view to improved management and restoration.25

Ensuring the Sustainable Use of Natural Resources and Preservation of Cultural
Heritage
Key challenges
Widespread poverty, rapid economic and population growth, and changes in the structure of production
are placing increasing stress on natural resources and biodiversity, particularly forest and land resources.
At the same time, natural resource management remains weak, and there is considerable misuse and waste
of both renewable and non-renewable resources, as well as inadequate use of potential opportunities and
comparative advantages. Knowledge and understanding of environmental and conservation issues are
limited at both the central and local levels. It is essential that natural resources are managed and utilized
in a proper manner, so that their potential can be fully harnessed for sustainable development. The
country’s biodiversity (flora and fauna) must be adequately protected and conserved. It is also essential to
protect and preserve the Lao unique cultural and historic heritage for future generations.
UNDAF support
The optimal and sustainable use of natural resources to ensure higher productivity, enhanced food security
and higher incomes at the household level is seen by the Government as an important means for achieving
the overarching goal of sustained growth with equity. The UN System, BWIs and ADB will provide
coordinated support to the implementation of sustainable forestry policies and logging practices,
introduction of diversified farming systems, and modernization of the agricultural sector. The UN
Country Team interventions will aim at developing and enforcing the effective and comprehensive natural
resource laws and regulations, and promoting adequate investment in the exploration of forest, water,
land and mineral resources. A particular effort will be made to increase community involvement in
natural resource planning and management, integrating public and private sector activities. UNESCO will
lead the UN support to conservation and preservation of the Lao PDR’s rich and unique cultural heritage,
including Luang Prabang, Vat Phou, and the Plain of Jars.
D. Human Rights, Gender Equality and Good Governance
Millennium Declaration Goals
Success, in meeting the objectives of development and poverty elimination depends, inter alia, on good
governance within each country.
We will spare no effort to promote democracy and strengthen the rule of law, as well as respect for all
internationally recognized human rights and fundamental freedoms, including the right to development.
We resolve therefore to strengthen the capacity of all our countries to implement the principles and
practices of democracy and respect for human rights.
National development goals
General human rights – The fundamental rights of Lao citizens and foreigners living in the Lao PDR will
be guaranteed on the basis of the laws and regulations. Social justice will be ensured to the multi-ethnic
peoples, giving them the opportunity to develop themselves and the society.26
Child protection – The Government will work towards meeting the goals of the UN Convention on the
Rights of the Child and the UN Declaration on Child Survival, Development and Protection: to ensure a
quality basic EFA (especially girls, and children of all ethnic groups), to reduce IMR, U5MR and MMR,
to expand immunization and improve reproductive health and safe delivery practices, to improve the

of HIV/AIDS and cross-border migration issues.27
Youth issues – The goal of the Lao Youth Union is to enhance, through skills development, information

towards the underprivileged regions, the Government’s quest for equitable ethnic representation will

Rural development – The ‘Focal Site’ approach was adopted by the Government in 1994 as the basis of

D.1. Promoting Human Rights for All
Millennium Declaration Goals
We resolve:
♦ To respect fully and uphold the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
♦ To strive for the full protection and promotion in all our countries of civil, political, economic, social
and cultural rights for all.
Key challenges
The United Nations Charter and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights clearly state the economic,
social, political, religious, cultural and family rights as integral parts of the international legal framework.
Whilst many important human rights and fundamental freedoms are guaranteed under the Lao
Constitution, national laws, and international multilateral instruments to which the Lao PDR is a State
party, some rights have not been fully put into practice. There is a need to create enabling conditions and
to strengthen people’s awareness of these rights to ensure universal access to equality and justice before
the law, and to make certain that human rights are fully incorporated into the aims and objectives of
national development planning and implementation.
In recent years, in the Lao PDR there has been increased acknowledgement of the international human
rights agenda, including the rights and fundamental freedoms embodied in the Universal Declaration of
Human Rights and various international declarations, covenants and conventions which form the basis of
the global UN mandate. As part of the celebrations of the 50th anniversary of the UDHR, the Declaration
and other international conventions were translated into Lao language for general distribution. Efforts
were made to implement and disseminate information on a number of critical treaties, including CEDAW
and CRC. In December 2000 the Lao PDR signed the International Covenant on Civil and Political
Rights and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights.
UNDAF support
As outlined in its core mandate, the UN System in collaboration with the Government and development
assistance partners will advocate for the goals and commitments contained in multilateral treaties,
international conventions and declarations to which the Lao PDR is a State party. The specific objectives
include strengthening national ownership of multilateral treaty commitments, incorporating treaty
provisions into the national legislative and planning processes, and assisting in their implementation. As
part of the overall UN effort to enhance institutional and human resource capacity of all branches of the
Government, capacity-building support will be provided to the Department of Treaties and Legal Affairs,
MOFA. In order to improve dissemination, enforcement of and reporting on the treaty obligations, and to
develop a sustainable, coherent and effective coordination in their implementation, the UN intends to
assist with establishing a documentation centre geared towards treaty related information, as well as
translating treaties into Lao language.
D.2. Improving Child Rights and Care and Reducing Child and Youth Vulnerability
Millennium Declaration/Development Goals
To have reduced by two thirds, between 1990 and 2015, the under-five child mortality.
We resolve to encourage the ratification and full implementation of the Convention on the Rights of the
Child and its optional protocols on the involvement of children in armed conflict and on the sale of
children, child prostitution and child pornography.
We also resolve to develop and implement strategies that give young people everywhere a real chance to
find decent and productive work.United Nations Development Assistance Framework for the Lao PDR 2002-2006
46
Key challenges
Despite significant improvements in mother and child health care and in primary education enrolment
over the past two decades, the rates for maternal, infant and under-five mortality remain extremely high.
Many children face chronic or acute malnutrition and/or remain outside the primary education system.
Capacities for understanding and responding to children with special learning and physical needs are still
at an embryonic stage. There is not yet a juvenile justice code or system to comprehensively protect
children. Lao youth is increasingly at risk from labour exploitation, sexual exploitation and trafficking,
HIV/AIDS infection, and illegal drug and substance abuse. It must be ensured that children’s rights are
fully secured and that all children and youth not only receive adequate health care and education but are
also protected from abuse and exploitation.
UNDAF support
UNICEF will lead the UN Country Team’s support to the Government in achieving the important goal of
improving child rights and care, and reducing child and youth vulnerability. The development goals
outlined in the Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989) and set at the World Summit for Children
(New York, 1990) will remain the bedrocks of UN work with the Government in this area. Related
objectives are of a multi-sectoral nature: legal protection and social justice; mother and child health; basic
education; and protection from drug abuse, HIV/AIDS and UXO, including regional dimensions.
The UN will focus on strengthening social networks, juvenile justice and child protection, eliminating
child labour, and preventing sexual exploitation and abuse (e.g. recently launched joint UN programme
on the elimination of trafficking in women and children in the Mekong sub-region). Assistance will be
targeted at mothers and children, for making motherhood safer and improving village-based early
childhood development/ care through expanded immunization, polio surveillance and IMCI programmes.
The UN, WB and ADB interventions will help to provide children and youth, in particular girls, with
better access to basic and non-formal education, vocational and life skills training, knowledge of
reproductive health, sexuality and population issues. Through a collaborative effort with national and
donor partners (including LCDC, NCCA and UXO LAO), the UN Country Team will disseminate
information, education and communication messages raising awareness of the dangers of drugs,
HIV/AIDS and UXO.
D.3. Ensuring Growth with Equity (Reducing Disparities)
Although the Government is committed to growth with equity, the Lao society is still marked by
considerable social and economic disparities, which restrict a large proportion of the population from
taking part in, and benefiting from, socio-economic growth and development. There is also evidence that
such disparities are increasing, as economic growth is not progressing in a uniform manner. Population
determinants partly explain the disparities between urban and rural areas and between men and women in
key social and economic indicators.
Gender Disparities
Millennium Declaration/Development Goals
To eliminate gender disparity in primary and secondary education preferably by 2005, and to all levels of
education no later than 2015.
We resolve to promote gender equality and the empowerment of women as effective ways to combat
poverty, hunger and disease and to stimulate development that is truly sustainable.
We also resolve to combat all forms of violence against women and to implement the Convention on the
Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women.United Nations Development Assistance Framework for the Lao PDR 2002-2006
47
Key challenges
From birth and through adulthood, girls and women in the Lao PDR do not often enjoy the same access to
opportunities as boys and men. In some areas, girls are often required to stay at home to undertake
household duties, especially in poor households or in large families, while boys are given priority to
enroll at school. The discrepancy between the enrolment of boys and girls in education increases through
secondary and tertiary levels. Illiteracy is markedly higher among women. An uneducated girl child will
become an illiterate mother and, therefore, less likely to undergo safe motherhood, improve family
nutrition, hygiene and health care or contribute to family income generation. Although female
involvement in leadership roles and decision-making at the family, village and national levels has
increased, it remains limited in many areas. Women do not have equal opportunity to access the
employment and remuneration. The right to ownership placed on legal ownership documents is in the
name of the ‘head of household’, usually the man.
It is essential that the considerable gender disparities that exist are addressed and that women be
encouraged to exercise their right to equality as guaranteed by the Constitution and international law
instruments. Steps must be taken to improve the access of girls and women to education, health and
reproductive health care services, employment opportunities and equal remuneration and ownership. It is
also important to ensure women's full and equal participation in decision-making processes and power
sharing at all levels, and to promote awareness of their contribution to the economy and their role in
managing natural resources and safeguarding the environment.
Ethnic Disparities
Millennium Declaration Goals
We resolve to strengthen the capacity of all our countries to implement the principles and practices of
democracy and respect for human rights, including minority rights.
Key challenges
The Lao PDR is an ethnically diverse country, with some 47 officially recognized ethnic groups.
Although comparatively small ethnic groups are present in every province, they are predominantly
concentrated in remote and/or inaccessible rural areas that have limited opportunities for economic
development. Significant disparities exist between ethnic groups in terms of access to and utilization of
education and health services and the attainment of literacy. Lack of educational materials in Lao and
other ethnic languages means that students spend time at school with little comprehension of the
instruction, resulting in high repetition rates. Ethnic groups inhabiting remote areas have less knowledge
of the three basic hygiene patters (eating, drinking, living) and more limited access to health care and
basic services, including water and sanitation. They, therefore, tend to experience significant disease
outbreaks and lower immunization rates leading to higher rates of maternal, infant and under-five
mortality.
In order for equitable development to take place it is essential to strengthen and improve measures aimed
at addressing the considerable ethnic disparities that exist. All people, irrespective of their race, colour,
descent or ethnic origin, must have the opportunity to exercise equal rights as guaranteed by the
Constitution and international law instruments. It is essential to improve all ethnic groups' access to
health and reproductive health care services, employment opportunities and education. The latter will
include the development of appropriate methods of teaching Lao to children speaking other ethnic
languages, this matter will be addressed in an ongoing research study to learn from and build on
experience. It is also imperative to ensure their full and equal participation in decision-making processes
and power sharing at all levels.United Nations Development Assistance Framework for the Lao PDR 2002-2006
48
Regional Disparities
Millennium Declaration Goals
We resolve to take measures to ensure respect for and protection of the human rights of migrants, migrant
workers and their families.
Key challenges
The Lao PDR suffers significant economic disparities between regions, provinces, districts, villages,
lowland-upland and urban-rural areas. Poverty is generally more widespread in remote upland areas.
Rural areas have lower incomes, higher food insecurity and malnutrition levels, and experience higher
rates of mortality, lower levels of education attainment, and lower opportunities for economic
advancement. This causes migration from rural to urban areas.
Regional disparities are particularly marked when comparing the relatively poor northern provinces with
the relatively rich lowland areas along the Mekong corridor, especially Vientiane Municipality.
Noticeable disparities exist between urban and rural areas and between different regions in terms of access
to and utilization of social infrastructure and services: roads and markets, health and education, water and
sanitation, and electricity. Unless such disparities are addressed in the immediate term, rural
communities and remoter provinces, districts and villages will have less chance to contribute to or benefit
from socio-economic growth.
Returnee Disparities
Millennium Declaration Goals
We resolve to strengthen international cooperation to help all refugees and displaced persons to return
voluntarily to their homes, in safety and dignity, and to be smoothly reintegrated into their societies.
Key challenges
By the end of 2000, 29,068 refugees had been repatriated to the Lao PDR, predominantly from Thailand
and China. Although all returnees received a basic package of repatriation assistance from UNHCR,
some of them continue to struggle for self-sufficiency. Even though the assistance given may appear to
have put the returnees above the level of their neighbours, many returnees have in fact fared worse than
their neighbours, primarily because they lack sufficient access to land that will enable them to feed their
families. This is the case for both group returnees, who received land donated by local villages, as well
as for individual family returnees, who have had to buy, rent or borrow land. A tendency of viewing the
responsibility for returnee villages as belonging to the MLSW and UNHCR has resulted in the exclusion
of many returnee villages from other development plans. As part of the Government’s efforts to assist
returnees, the MOFA, MOI and MLSW address the needs of returnee villages through special
development plans.
In order for equitable development to take place, efforts must be made to reduce the inequities
experienced by returnee families and guarantee them equitable access to development plans, income
generating opportunities and social services.
UNDAF support to reduce disparities
The UN System, BWIs and ADB fully share the Government’s commitment to the vision of sustained
growth with equity, which translates into the development programmes aiming to reduce the existing
gender, ethnic, regional and returnee disparities. The UN will continue to target its assistance at the most
vulnerable and poor with a focus on overcoming the social and economic disparities. Coordinated efforts
will be made to improve the access of girls, women and ethnic groups inhabiting remote areas, to
education, health and reproductive health care services, employment opportunities, equal remunerationUnited Nations Development Assistance Framework for the Lao PDR 2002-2006
49
and ownership. It is also imperative to promote their equal participation in decision-making processes,
and contribution to the economic growth and natural resource management. The UN Country Team will
provide specific support to build capacity for integrated rural development to eliminate disparities between
rural-urban and upland-lowland areas. As another immediate objective, aiming at reducing the inequities
experienced by returnee families, the UN and its partners will take measures to absorb returnee sites in
the existing or planned development programmes, to ensure consistent follow-up upon UNHCR phaseout.
UNHCR Phase-out
During 2001 UNHCR has gradually phased-out most of its work in the Lao PDR, brining to
conclusion over 25 years of reintegration activities and protection monitoring of returnees.
In the last 15 years, and particularly since 1990, UNHCR has initiated and completed
reintegration activities for 29,000 people, concentrating primarily on small and large group
villages. Assistance included: 1) construction of irrigation systems, roads, schools, dispensaries,
latrines, and water supply systems; 2) training of teachers and village health volunteers,
provision of revolving funds and vocational skills training; and 3) community development
activities in agriculture, education and health provided through the implementing NGO partners.
Protection activities focused on monitoring returnees during and after return, as well as
investigating allegations of mistreatment of returnees.
UNHCR’s substantial activities ended in 2000, with the 2001 budget covering only some training
and emergency needs of particularly vulnerable returnee families. In view of eventual closure of
the UNHCR Branch Office in the Lao PDR, UNHCR continued its search for avenues for
increased inter–agency collaboration by the end of 2001. UNHCR identified a number of
villages with ongoing problems relating to health, education, or achievement of self-sufficiency.
In addition, given the lack of internal resources of the central and provincial Departments of
Social Welfare, future maintenance of the older UNHCR-constructed projects will be an
increasing problem.
In preparation for phasing-out, UNHCR initiated discussions with other UN agencies, NGOs,
and bilateral donors on the eventual hand over of both its development and human rights
responsibilities, to ensure that returnees enjoy equal rights and equitable access to development
plans, income generation opportunities, and social services. Although the resulting collaboration
was limited thus far (by differences in scope of projects, geographical emphasis, and planning
cycles), UNHCR will continue communication to seek sources for long-term development
assistance identified by the authorities and villagers.
National development goals
Participation and decentralization are integral elements of the national planning for poverty alleviation.
The participatory planning (i.e. “bottom-up”) approach chosen by the Government is a conscious effort to
empower provinces and districts to achieve and defend a vision, to identify the dynamics of the
development process that they would favour, and to coherently plan adequate responses to the people’s
aspirations as expressed by their close involvement in the planning process. As part of the new
decentralization policy, since March 2000, the provinces have become strategic units, the districts
planning and budgeting units, and the villages implementing units.
Human resource development is among the main national development priorities, along with achieving
permanent food security and preserving natural resources. Capacity building is one of the most
fundamental national needs, and for this reason, the Government has always insisted that all projectsUnited Nations Development Assistance Framework for the Lao PDR 2002-2006
50
funded by the international donor community contain an important capacity and institutional building
component. Capacity building for public management and community development is given the top
priority. The national HRD programme combines in an integrated way (1) the institutional strengthening,
with (2) improved individual capabilities, to ensure (3) a wider social outreach of participatory community
development, with ethnic minorities, women and children as the privileged target groups.
Governance is at the heart of the Lao PDR’s move towards sustainable human and economic
development. The Government considers governance as a vital link between economic growth and
poverty reduction, and as an essential condition for moving beyond the status of a LDC by the year 2020.
Consequently, great emphasis has been placed on the Governance and Public Administration Reform
(GPAR) programme32 (refer to section D.10. “Towards Better Governance” in chapter II).
Data, information and knowledge – Consideration must be given to the establishment of a science,
technology and environment council, experiment, analysis and research centres in each sector and locality
in order to improve productivity, efficiency and quality of management. To conduct basic surveys to
provide data for the research and planning. To conduct researches and widely disseminate knowledge
about Lao language, literature, history, art and culture with an aim to promote understanding of the
national culture, and encourage innovative cultural products and activities.33
D.4. Deepening Participation and Broadening Partnerships
Millennium Declaration Goals
We resolve to develop strong partnerships with the private sector and with civil society organizations in
pursuit of development and poverty eradication.
We also resolve to work collectively for more inclusive political processes, allowing genuine participation
by all citizens in all our countries.
Key challenges
For development activities to be successful they must be reflective of and responsive to people’s needs.
In line with the Government efforts towards decentralization and improved provincial capacity, strategic
planning and development processes have been promoted at the provincial level. It is essential to ensure
well implemented, ‘bottom-up’ participatory planning, in which all stakeholders, public and private,
national and local, are fully involved in all stages of development planning, implementation and
assessment. There is also a need to strengthen the existing ties and explore new avenues for partnerships
with the private sector, civil society organizations, NGOs and the development assistance community.
UNDAF support
The UN Country Team is committed to assist the Government in deepening people’s participation and
broadening partnerships in development. The UN support will specifically aim at building national
capacity required for effective decentralization of planning, management and budget responsibilities to
enable greater participation by the provinces, districts and villages. An effort will be made to institute
stronger mechanisms for leveling regional income disparities and reducing poverty through an incentivebased revenue generation system at local levels. The UN programmes will contribute to increasing
individuals’ access to information and education to enable meaningful participation in development, as
well as to promoting partnerships with the private sector, civil society and community-based
organizations.

D.5. Building Institutional and Administrative Capacity
Key challenges
Good governance forms the basis for sustainable development and the effective allocation of resources.
Despite progress, institutional structures and administrative and management capacity in the Lao PDR
remain weak. Monitoring and reporting of Government’s expenditure and resources are inadequate.
There is a need to develop effective, transparent and accountable operational mechanisms and procedures
at all levels and sectors of the Government. Public institutions need to be transformed into demandorientated service providers. Other priorities are to speed up decision-making processes, ensure meritbased promotion and develop effective mechanisms that encourage fair practice.
UNDAF support
The UN System and its partners remain dedicated to the goal of strengthening institutional structures and
administrative and management capacity. In this core governance area, the main UN objectives are:
strengthening the legal framework; affirming the National Assembly legislative and political role;
developing the Government’s capacity and institutional memory in relation to signing, ratifying and
reporting on treaty obligations; improving transparency, accountability and operational efficiency; and
promoting the role of a civil society. The UN Country Team will coordinate and complement agencyspecific capacity building efforts in many areas from disaster management, agriculture and extension, to
microfinance, rural credit, and private financing of industrial infrastructure.
D.6. Strengthening Human Resource Capacity
Key challenges
The Lao PDR is critically short of the ‘social capital’ required for development. There is a general lack
of well-educated and experienced personnel at all levels of society and in all sectors. This poses a serious
constraint on development in the Lao PDR. Moreover, as efforts are made to develop a sustainable
human resource base, the demand for qualified, skilled or appropriately trained personnel, particularly
managers, is ever increasing due to rapid economic progress.
There is an urgent need to make sustainable improvements in both the numbers of trained people and in
the quality of training. The development of such resources will require focusing national development
efforts on health, formal and non-formal education, and vocational skills training. This should begin with
maternal health and early childhood development and continue right through adulthood. Human resource
development activities must be closely linked to the future needs and requirements of both the public and
private sectors. Strengthened human resource capacity in all stages of development activities would
reduce dependency on external technical assistance.
UNDAF support
Recognizing a priority need for sustainable development of human resources, the UN Country Team will
assist the Government in the adoption of a comprehensive strategic approach to HRD in all sectors and at
all levels, and improvement of human resource planning to ensure an optimal utilization of the ‘social
capital’. The UN will particularly focus on adapting the training curriculum to meet the current and
anticipated future needs of the labour market, and encouraging private sector involvement in curriculum
design and vocational skills training. Other important objectives include: skills development (language,
general knowledge, life, vocational and technical), quality assurance, and supporting the Government’s
efforts to enhance staff motivation and create greater incentives for the civil service.United Nations Development Assistance Framework for the Lao PDR 2002-2006
52
D.7. Improving the Collection, Analysis and Dissemination of Data, Information and
Knowledge
Key challenges
The availability of data, information and knowledge underpins development planning, responsive
decision-making, and effective assessment and monitoring of progress at all levels and in all sectors.
Whilst both the quantity and reliability of national and sub-national data continue to improve, there is still
a critical lack of quantitative and qualitative gender disaggregated data in many key areas, such as national
expenditure, poverty and HIV/AIDS. Mechanisms for information collection, analysis, transfer,
dissemination and absorption are extremely limited and lack coordination. It is essential to make both
quantitative and qualitative improvements in data availability to enhance development interventions. The
establishment of information networks would allow people, especially key groups such as farmers and
businessmen, access to commercial and market information.
UNDAF support
Recognizing the important need for improving mechanisms and capacities for collection, analysis and
dissemination of data, information and knowledge, the UN Country Team will aim at strengthening the
national surveillance, statistical and operational research capacities to ensure effective and efficient data
collection, analysis and projection. The analysis and mapping of national data using Geographical
Information System is seen as a relevant tool to better understand geographical and socio-economic
differences and parallels among provinces, districts and villages. The GIS technology will also be applied
for the establishment of an early warning system for disaster preparedness. As per its core mandate, the
UN will follow-up on national progress in achieving the world conferences targets, and provide support to
fulfilling the national commitments and reporting requirements under world conferences and multilateral
treaties, including WSC, UNCED, ICPD, WSSD, FWCW, WFS, UNGASS on the World Drug Problem
and HIV/AIDS, and the Millennium Summit, which directly relate to the UN poverty eradication and
human rights goals.United Nations Development Assistance Framework for the Lao PDR 2002-2006

IV. Cooperation Strategies
UNDAF Principles
The UN Country Team in the Lao PDR will be guided by the following principles deriving from the
UNDAF, when developing and implementing their individual programmes of cooperation. The UN will:
• Support the national development priorities and goals set by the Government.
• Support the Lao PDR’s progress in realizing the goals and commitments emanating from the
Millennium Declaration, world conferences and multilateral treaties, in the overall context of the
Global Agenda for Development.
• Promote national ownership of programmes and projects through sustainable capacity building and
enabling people’s participation.
• Apply human rights-based approach to development that
- focuses on people as holders of rights, as well as duties and responsibilities;
- adopts the fundamental principles of non-discrimination;
- prioritizes needs of the most disadvantaged and vulnerable;
- reiterates that development is a human right; and
- targets the goal of poverty eradication by addressing structural inequalities that cause poverty.34
• Mainstream gender issues and promote gender equality.
• Incorporate sub-regional and regional issues into development programmes to enable the Lao PDR’s
regional and global integration.
• Implement actions of the UN Secretary-General’s Programme for Reform (14 July 1997) to enhance
inter-agency coordination/ collaboration in both operational and programme matters.
• Pursue meaningful partnerships among all development stakeholders: the Government, UN System,
BWIs, ADB, bi- and multilateral donors, civil society, and the private sector.
A. Strategic Approaches for Collaboration
The UN agency collaboration in the Lao PDR will take a form of a mix of agency-specific,
complementary, parallel, and joint programmes and projects (for definitions, refer to chapter V “Followup and Review”). The UN Country Team will review opportunities for developing parallel and joint
programmes where they add value, while the prevailing form of UN agency collaboration will be a set of
agency-specific or complementary programmes.
Strategic approaches for UN collaboration in achieving the four major goals – development and poverty
eradication policies and strategies; response to basic human needs; sustainable use of natural resources
and preservation of cultural heritage; and human rights, gender equality and good governance – will vary
for each development intervention. In course of the UNDAF preparation, the UN Country Team
identified tentative cooperation strategies in most areas, which will be further detailed and strengthened
during the implementation, follow-up and review stages. A selection of UN cooperation strategies

Ongoing joint UN programmes/ projects in the Lao PDR
HIV/AIDS Trust Fund
The Lao HIV/AIDS Trust Fund formed in 1998, assists the Government in mobilizing and
coordinating resources for the implementation of the National Plan on HIV/AIDS/STI 1997-
2001. The TF also serves as a mechanism to ensure that resources are used effectively to
develop a comprehensive national strategy to prevent HIV/AIDS reaching the high levels found
in neighbouring countries. The TF has a broad range of partners, including the key line
ministries, UN System, donors, NGOs, all Lao mass organizations, and the PCCAs established
in every province, supported by the HIV/AIDS Theme Group.United Nations Development Assistance Framework for the Lao PDR 2002-2006

National UXO Trust Fund
The UXO Trust Fund established in 1995, is the main funding mechanism for UXO LAO – the
Lao National Programme for UXO Clearance and Awareness. The UN assists the Government
to manage and administer the TF. Annual audits are conducted to ensure full transparency and
accountability. The annual budget for UXO LAO is approximately US$ 9.5 million, including
equipment and international support costs. Current TF’s donors include: Australia, Belgium,
Canada, Denmark, EU, Finland, Germany, Japan, the Lao PDR, Luxembourg, Netherlands,

Handicap International and the Belgian Military are the six UXO LAO implementing partners.

The Joint UN Alternative Development project in Nonghet, Xieng Khouang province, launched
by UNDCP, UNDP, UNICEF, UNFPA, FAO, WFP, UNAIDS and IFAD in 1997, represents
not only the first UN joint programming effort, but also the first UNDCP nationally-executed
project in the Lao PDR. It addresses a number of national development priorities, and focuses
UN System support on the reduction of opium production and consumption among ethnic groups
in highland areas. As agreed during the joint programme formulation, UN agency contributions
are based on the experiences and competencies of specific agencies, with UNDCP playing a lead
role in drug control activities, and UNDP providing administrative support.
UN Project on Eliminating Trafficking in Women and Children in the Mekong Sub-region
The UN project on Eliminating Trafficking in Women and Children signed in 2000, is one of a
number of initiatives currently being undertaken by UN agencies, Governments, NGOs and
community-based organizations to combat the problem of trafficking in women and children in
the Mekong sub-region. The project provides the UN System (including UNAIDS, UNICEF,
UNDP, UNFPA, UNDCP, UNHCR, UNESCO, ILO and ESCAP), in partnership with the
Governments and other concerned organizations, with an overarching mechanism to coordinate
local, national and sub-regional activities through a multi-disciplinary participatory approach.
The project covers Cambodia, China, Lao PDR, Thailand and Vietnam. UNDP and UNICEF
share the focal point responsibilities for the project.

The UN Country Team in the Lao PDR employs several regular mechanisms for inter-agency
coordination and collaboration to ensure more integrated, complementary action at the country level
related to both programme and administrative matters. On the programme side, the main instruments for
UN collaboration include the monthly UN Country Team (UNCT) meetings, and the UN theme/working

meet monthly to discuss and streamline administrative/ operational procedures. The UN Security
Management Team (SMT) chaired by the UN Designated Official for Security also meets on a monthly

The UN Country Team, consisting of the heads of UN agencies, BWIs, and ADB (that joined the team in

serve as a practical forum for developing joint UN actions and strategies. Every year the UN Country

of preparation of the RC Annual Report and the Country Team self-assessment exercises. The UN
Country Team also directly managed the UNDAF process.
UNDAF Monitoring Group
The UNDAF Monitoring Group, consisting of the UNDAF focal points at each agency, will be

V. Follow-up and Review
The UNDAF is intended to serve as a strategic planning framework, providing the overall mission and
direction of UN development assistance to the Lao PDR during the next five years (2002-2006). It must,
therefore, be a living document, able to adapt itself to better respond to the country’s development
challenges in a changing environment. This chapter describes how the UNDAF provisions will be
implemented, monitored, reviewed and revised through the individual agency country programmes and
projects, as well as complementary mechanisms and processes.
The key follow-up and review actions are outlined below, whilst the UN Country Team may develop
more concrete and detailed actions and approaches during the actual implementation and in outcome of the
regular review, monitoring and evaluation.
A. UNDAF Implementation and Follow-up
A.1. Harmonization of Programme Cycles
The individual country cooperation programmes of UN organizations usually vary in duration and type.
In the Lao PDR, in response to the General Assembly Resolution No. 47/199, and in order to ensure an
overall improvement in the effectiveness and efficiency of the UN System, the UN funding agencies
(UNDP, UNICEF, UNFPA and WFP) held extensive discussions, and by October 1999 reached an
agreement on the harmonization their programme cycles.
UNFPA and UNDP agreed that their future programme cycles should be extended to five-year cycles in
line with those of UNICEF. UNFPA and UNDP agreed to extend their current programme cycles by one
year until December 2001, whilst UNICEF agreed to shorten its existing programme cycle by one year
until December 2001. All three agencies then agreed to commence five-year programme cycles,
beginning in January 2002 and ending in December 2006. With regard to WFP, it has been in the process
of switching from a mainly emergency focused operation to a longer-term development programme. Any
future programme cycles developed by WFP will take into account the harmonized programme cycles of
UNICEF, UNFPA and UNDP. All four funding agencies will thus start a new programme cycle
coinciding with the duration of the UNDAF from 2002-2006.
A.2. Development and Implementation of Programmes and Projects of the UN System
Organizations
The most important challenge upon completion of the UNDAF is to ensure that its provisions are reflected
in cooperation between the UN System and the programme country. This task will be carried out through
the programming processes of participating UN organizations, which are led by the Government and
involve other development partners. These processes must also provide opportunities for inter-agency
consultation and involvement.
In terms of content, successful follow-up requires a number of measures, as described below.
• The selection and definition of goals, objectives and intervention strategies as well as the pattern of
resource allocation in the programmes and projects of individual organizations must be consistent with
the UNDAF. The texts of individual country programme and project documents will, therefore,
specify how the UNDAF has been addressed by UN System organizations.United Nations Development Assistance Framework for the Lao PDR 2002-2006
62
• Proposals within the UNDAF for any potential parallel or joint programming initiatives should be
followed up and incorporated into programmes or projects. This is essential for achieving one of the
principal objectives of the UNDAF, which is to enhance the effectiveness of the UN System through
collaborative action.
The UN Development Group’s definitions of programming modalities36
Agency programme
Programme resulting from a formulation process specific to one agency, addressing a need
identified through a collaborative assessment and strategic programme development process.
Rationale, objectives, activities and outputs are described in one document, which includes a
budget necessary to achieve the objectives. Such programmes and projects should nevertheless
be responsive to the strategic objectives of the UNDAF and the document should provide clear
statements to that effect.
Parallel programme
Programme of two or more organizations deriving from common problem identification, as well
as a shared overall strategy for concerted action. Activities are reflected by each agency in selfreliant/comprehensive documents which complement each other, with specific reference to one
another. The monitoring and evaluation of parallel programmes is done jointly by the
participating agencies.
Joint programme
Programme of two or more agencies resulting from a joint programming process. Within the
context of approved agency country programmes and signed agreements, the programme is
outlined in a single document, which describes the linkages between and responsibilities of all
participating agencies.
• Whether cooperation is undertaken individually, in parallel or jointly, the UN System, working in
collaboration with the Government, needs to employ the programme approach and national execution
as preferred modalities. Concerted efforts will be made by the UN organizations to build national
institutional and administrative capacities and strengthen human resources, as a matter of priority.
In terms of process,
• UN theme/working groups described in chapter IV B. above will contribute to soliciting the inputs
and participation of UN System organizations and development partners in the UNDAF
implementation and follow-up.
• Prior to submission of individual country programmes to governing bodies, the UN Country Team
should undertake a country-level review of proposed activities to ensure consistency with the goals
and objectives of the UNDAF. Where required by organisational procedures and structures, or in the
case of organizations not represented locally, this will be achieved through consultation with the
Headquarters and/or regional offices of individual organizations.
• Finally, the UNDAF will be brought to the attention of governing bodies in connection with the
submission of individual country programmes or other similar documents.

A.3. Advocacy and Policy Dialogue
Using the UNDAF as a platform, advocacy and policy dialogue can focus on:
• The evolving country situation and its implications for development cooperation, especially the role of
the UN System;
• Better integration of the UN development assistance with the national policies, plans and programmes,
facilitated through application of the programme approach;
• The UN System support for the follow-up to the global development agenda emerging from the UN
world conferences, declarations and international conventions to which the Lao PDR is a State party;
• Agreement on and definition of the UN System’s participation in sector investment programmes
(SIPs) and sector-wide approaches (SWAPs); and
• Clearer communication to bilateral and multilateral donors, civil society, private sector and other
partners on the UN’s special role and impact within development cooperation.
A.4. Support to the Government in Aid Coordination and Resource Mobilization
The CCA and UNDAF processes have a potential to generate value-added in ways that enable the UN
System to better support aid coordination. The added value can emerge from the establishment of
stronger partnerships, increased networking among development organizations, greater exchange of
information and expertise, and more focused and collaborative UN System participation in development
cooperation.
UN organizations can build upon these assets to support the Government in aid coordination on an
ongoing basis through, for example, the use of thematic groups and organisation of multi-donor missions
and joint evaluations. Reviews of the UNDAF, as part of the regular processes of programme reviews
and the Resident Coordinator System reporting procedures, will contribute to the Round Table process,
by offering additional opportunities for bringing together a wide range of partners to discuss major
development issues and future donor support to the country.
The UNDAF follow-up will also provide an opportunity to secure additional resources in support of the
national needs and priorities. This can be achieved through the improved UN System support to the
Government’s participation in the Round Table process and policy dialogues, as well as through
individual and joint fundraising efforts.
A.5. Streamlining and Simplification of Procedures
The General Assembly resolution 53/192 calls for further simplification, harmonization and
rationalization of procedures for operational activities of the United Nations development system at the
field level in consultation with national Governments. It also urges the funds and programmes to put in
place specific measures and timetables to advance the simplification and harmonization of procedures, and
to report on these to their respective governing bodies.
The UNDAF should ultimately contribute to this streamlining of procedures by simplifying the
requirements of individual organizations for programming and operational processes. This result will,
however, be obtained only when existing rules, regulations and procedures are adequately reformed by
UN System organizations in favour of simplification and harmonization at the system level.37 While
progress is expected in this area in the immediate future, the UN Country Team will continue to look for
efficient ways to simplify and harmonize their programming and operational procedures, within the

context of existing rules and procedures, in order to provide a more effective system-wide response to the
local needs and conditions.
A.6. Establishment of Follow-up Arrangements
Effective follow-up on the UNDAF requires the establishment of adequate mechanisms for sustained
dialogue, planning and review among the Government, UN System and other development partners. Such
mechanisms will be based upon the arrangements already in place within the Resident Coordinator
System, including the UN Country Team, UN theme/working groups, Office of the Resident Coordinator,
Quarterly Donor Meetings, UN Security Management Team, Inter-Agency Admin. Officers meetings,
electronic website of the UN System in the Lao PDR, and most importantly, the UNDAF Monitoring
Group. Smaller theme/working groups can be further established around specific issues, as the needs and
opportunities arise.
The UNDAF Monitoring Group with the involvement of the Government and key development partners
will be charged with the role of following-up on all matters related to the implementation of the provisions
of the UNDAF. It will be formed by the UNDAF focal points identified within each participating
agency, and will report its findings and recommendations directly to the UN Country Team. The Country
Team is committed to encourage the respective agency staff, assigned as the UNDAF focal points, to
dedicate themselves to this important task.
More specifically, the UNDAF Monitoring Group will have the following responsibilities:
! To map all ongoing and planned activities of the UN System organizations and facilitate cross-agency
information sharing on these activities. As an immediate challenge, the monitoring group will need to
identify mechanisms and measures to improve the gathering and sharing of development information
among agencies and with the key partners, potentially leading to better coordination;
! To monitor the UNDAF correlation with the national development needs, priorities and programmes
that emerge, and make recommendations on any revisions and modifications be made to the UNDAF
objectives and matrix, in order to ensure effective support to the national development goals;
! To carry out annual and mid-term reviews of the UNDAF, as well as the final evaluation, and submit
findings to the UN Country Team;
! To explore possibilities for the development of joint and parallel programmes/ projects on the basis of
the UNDAF, and plan and recommend any collaborative initiatives of both policy and localized
nature;
! To assist with the integration of UNDAF goals and principles in all UN System organizations’
programmes and activities;
! To identify the needs and possibilities for harmonizing and streamlining the agency programming and
operational procedures and processes to avoid duplication, multiple requirements and the imposition
of an unnecessary burden on both the Government and UN organizations;
! To thoroughly coordinate the UNDAF-related tasks with, and call for the assistance and inputs from,
the UN theme/working groups;
! To coordinate the UNDAF review, monitoring and evaluation with the Millennium Development
Goals reporting (MDGR) exercise to ensure consistency and complementarity of both processes. The
MDGR will also contribute important targets for assessing the UNDAF progress; and
! At all times, to act as UNDAF resource persons and advocates within each respective UN
organization.United Nations Development Assistance Framework for the Lao PDR 2002-2006

The UNDAF Monitoring Group will further detail and sharpen its responsibilities, and identify a meeting
schedule in agreement with the UN Country Team.
B. UNDAF Monitoring and Evaluation
The UN System organizations participating in the UNDAF, led by the Resident Coordinator, bear the
responsibility for the monitoring and evaluation of the UNDAF in close partnership with the Government.
The basic principles and requirements outlined below derive from the UNDAF Guidelines and apply to all
countries where UNDAFs exist. The UN Country Team and UNDAF Monitoring Group intend to
further determine more specific modalities and arrangements in the context of UNDAF Lao PDR.
B.1. Basic Principles for Monitoring and Evaluation of the UNDAF
In general, monitoring and evaluation activities should focus on:
• The extent to which the UNDAF has fulfilled its basic purpose, as stated by the Secretary-General in
Action 10 (a)38, in General Assembly resolution 53/19239, and further elaborated in the UNDAF
Guidelines, section 2;
• The extent of progress towards the goals and objectives of the UNDAF, and lessons learnt;
• Progress towards more effective partnerships within the UN System and with the Government and
other development partners; and
• Progress in harmonization and streamlining of programming and operational procedures and
processes, to avoid multiple requirements and the imposition of an unnecessary burden on both the
Government and participating UN System organizations.
B.2. Monitoring
Monitoring of the UNDAF is crucial to ensure that it remains relevant to the national development needs
and priorities and continues to be an effective tool for enhanced UN System collaboration. In light of
this, regular reviews should be conducted to assess the progress of the UNDAF. Monitoring will also
help to identify issues that need to be addressed by forthcoming evaluations.
To the extent possible and in order to reduce the burden on the UN System, Government and partners,
monitoring should be carried out as an integral part of the existing procedures and processes of the UN
organizations. In particular, the following provide natural entry points for such review:
The preparation and review of the Workplans and Annual Reports of the Resident Coordinator
Based on findings of the annual reviews of country programmes or projects conducted by the UN
organizations (including findings on their contributions for meeting the UNDAF objectives), the UN
Country Team will normally assess the progress of UNDAF during the course of the preceding year, and
present the outcome of this exercise through the Annual Reports of the Resident Coordinator.

B.3. Evaluation
At the end of the UNDAF cycle, participating UN organizations in consultation with the Government will
organize an evaluation of the UNDAF with the primary purpose to:
• To examine the extent to which the UNDAF has fulfilled its basic purpose, as stated by the SecretaryGeneral in Action 10 (a), in General Assembly resolution 53/192, and further elaborated in the
UNDAF Guidelines, section 2; and
• To assess the achievement of all or selected UNDAF objectives, and take stock of the lessons learnt,
including well-validated practices that could be adopted for the subsequent UNDAF and similar
exercises.
Since the UNDAF emphasises the value of partnerships, it should be evaluated jointly. The UN System
organizations, in consultation with the Government, will determine the specific themes/topics to be
covered. For this purpose, terms of reference, including the focus of evaluation, should be elaborated
and agreed upon.
The UN organizations will however, as appropriate and necessary, continue to conduct evaluations of

C. Status of Development Cooperation in the Lao PDR
Following the launching of reforms under the NEM in 1986 and a sustained period of relatively stable
macroeconomic management, the Lao PDR was able to share many of the benefits of the “Asian
miracle”. Real economic growth averaged almost 7% per year from 1990 to 1997, and it appears that the
poor were among the most important beneficiaries, with the incidence of poverty falling from 45 to 39%
between 1992/93 and 1997/98.49 Nevertheless, the Lao PDR depends on many more years of such
growth to provide the conditions for continued poverty reduction.
Like all other countries throughout the South-East Asian region, the Lao economy suffered from the
negative effects of the Asian economic crisis. Although the agricultural sector provided some resiliency,
especially in the early stages of the crisis when world prices of rice remained high, the crisis had severe
impact on macroeconomic management. Major revenue shortfalls in the pubic sector, combined with the
large increases in off-budget public investment expenditure on rural infrastructure, led to serious and
largely unintended monetary and inflationary consequences.
The inflation rate began to accelerate in early 1998, reaching a peak of 167% in March 1999. Month to
month inflation rates remained high until August 1999. Monetary-induced inflation led to a massive fall
in the nominal value of the Kip and a smaller but significant decline in its real value. In July 1999 the
Kip reached its lowest point representing only 14.8% of it’s pre-crisis value relative to the Thai Baht.50
Strong fiscal and monetary measures, initiated in the final months of 1999, have laid the foundations for
renewed macroeconomic stability. Since September 1999 month to month inflation rates have remained
extremely low and sometimes negative, a trend now reflected in a declining annual inflation rate. The
Kip appreciated, in nominal and real terms, and has remained stable (relative to the Baht). However,
despite this commendable achievement, macroeconomic stabilization remains fragile, and further progress
is required to maintain recent hard-won gains.
The 7th Round Table Meeting (RTM) of development partners for the Lao PDR was organized jointly by
the Government and UNDP from 20-22 November 2000, attended by over 250 representatives of donor
countries, EU, multilateral financial institutions, UN System, and NGOs. For the first time the RTM was
held in Vientiane.
The Round Table in the Lao PDR has progressively evolved from an one time event towards an ongoing
cyclical process, involving stakeholder dialogue on national strategies for agriculture, rural development,
health, education, roads, forestry, and macroeconomic management, as well as aid management and
absorptive capacity issues. The development partners reaffirmed their commitment to support the Lao
PDR in alleviating poverty, and graduating from the LDC’s status by the year 2020. Many development
partners announced firm commitments in the form of loans and grant aid and made specific pledges
totaling approximately US$ 386 millions for the year 2001. This figure is higher than the commitments
made at the 6th RTM in 1997.
